item.description:
Introduction

Full-text search (FTS) is a powerful tool for efficiently navigating large datasets. This guide delves into the implementation of FTS3 and FTS4 extensions of SQLite on Android, showcasing their capabilities in searching for words, phrases, and wildcards within a text column.

Understanding FTS3 and FTS4

FTS3 and FTS4 extensions in SQLite enable robust full-text search functionality. FTS3, introduced in SQLite version 3.7.4 (2009), laid the foundation, while FTS4, unveiled in version 3.8.0 (2013), introduced support for an “external content table.” This external table optimizes storage by avoiding duplicate entries in the FTS table, making it particularly beneficial for large datasets.

item.title: Installing SQL*Plus Client in Linux
item.description:
How to Install SQL*Plus Client on CentOS to Connect with Oracle Server

If you’re working on AWS services and managing an ec2 CentOS instance, configuring the SQL*Plus client to connect with a remote Oracle server is a common requirement. This step-by-step guide will walk you through the installation process on CentOS.

  1. Visit the Oracle Linux x86-64 instant clients download page .
  2. Download the appropriate client for your Oracle server version. For example, for oracle-se(11.2.0.2), download:
    • oracle-instantclient11.2-basic-11.2.0.2.0.x86_64.rpm
    • oracle-instantclient11.2-sqlplus-11.2.0.2.0.x86_64.rpm
  3. Install the client using the following command:
    • rpm -ivh oracle-instantclient11.2-basic-11.2.0.2.0.x86_64.rpm
    • rpm -ivh oracle-instantclient11.2-sqlplus-11.2.0.2.0.x86_64.rpm
  4. Set environment variables in your ~/.bash_profile file:
    • ORACLE_HOME=/usr/lib/oracle/11.2/client64
    • PATH=$ORACLE_HOME/bin:$PATH
    • LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$ORACLE_HOME/lib
    • export ORACLE_HOME
    • export LD_LIBRARY_PATH
    • export PATH
  5. Reload your ~/.bash_profile by typing the command:
    • source ~/.bash_profile
  6. Connect to the remote Oracle server using SQL*Plus with the following command:
    • sqlplus "username/pass@(DESCRIPTION=(ADDRESS=(PROTOCOL=TCP)(HOST=192.168.2.1)(PORT=1521))(CONNECT_DATA=(SID=YOURSID)))"

Note: Replace “username,” “pass,” “HOST,” “PORT,” and “YOURSID” with your actual values.

item.title: Acquiring the Maximum Date in Oracle
item.description:
In Oracle, the maximum possible date that can be inserted into a date field is December 31, 9999 AD. This date can be obtained using the TO_DATE function and the correct format.

Code Explanation

To obtain the maximum possible date in Oracle, you can use the following code snippet:

SELECT TO_DATE('31.12.9999 23:59:59', 'dd.mm.yyyy hh24:mi:ss')
FROM dual;

This code uses the TO_DATE function to convert a string representation of the maximum date (‘31.12.9999 23:59:59’) to a date datatype. The format of the string is specified as ‘dd.mm.yyyy hh24:mi:ss’, indicating the day, month, year, hour, minute, and second. The result is then displayed using the SELECT statement.

item.title: Atomic Merge In Oracle Is It Possible
item.description:
Atomic MERGE in Oracle: Is it Possible?

Can I do an atomic MERGE in Oracle?

Yes and no. The MERGE statement in Oracle is inherently atomic, as the transactional control is wrapped around the entire statement. However, as with any database operation, concurrency issues may arise if multiple sessions attempt to merge the same records simultaneously.

Scenario Example:

Consider two instances of a J2EE app running in a WebLogic cluster. These apps perform a MERGE operation to insert or update a record in the Oracle database. The MERGE checks if a row with a specified primary key exists; if it does, it updates it, and if not, it inserts it.

item.title: Available Nosql Databases For Azure
item.description:
Available NoSQL Databases for Azure NoSQL Database Options for Azure

Introduction

When it comes to storing data for an Azure cloud app, SQL-Azure is a popular option. Although, if you are interested in exploring NoSQL options, this post will give you an overview of the available options and which ones are considered leaders in this space.

What NoSQL Options are Available for Azure?

If you’re looking for alternatives to SQL Azure, there are a few NoSQL options available. One of the most popular options is Windows Azure Table Storage APIs . This option provides a scalable, non-relational datastore that works with the .NET framework. It is a good option if you need a simple, key-value store that can handle massive amounts of data. Another option is Data Storage Offerings on the Windows Azure Platform . This offers a range of NoSQL services, including DocumentDB and Azure Cosmos DB. Both of these options are fully managed NoSQL databases that can scale elastically and handle data of any shape and size. They also offer support for different programming languages and frameworks. Lastly, some people run MongoDB within an Azure worker role. MongoDB is a popular NoSQL database that is known for its flexibility and scalability. It can handle a wide range of data types and provides amazing querying capabilities. Although, setting up and managing MongoDB on your own can be challenging, especially when it comes to configuring replica sets and managing scalability.

This Q&A Session will explain the reasons why a website would want to use a NoSQL database, with practical examples.

1. Better Performance

One of the key benefits of using a NoSQL database is better performance. This is because NoSQL databases do not require complex operations such as joins that can slow down SQL databases. Moreover, NoSQL databases provide a flexible schema that allows data to be stored in a simple and flexible format that can reduce data retrieval time.

Cx_Oracle serves as a Python extension module facilitating connections between Python and Oracle databases. Adhering to the Python database API 2.0 specification, it provides Oracle-specific features and performance enhancements.

Example:

import cx_Oracle

dsn_tns = cx_Oracle.makedsn('host', 'port', service_name='servicename') 
conn = cx_Oracle.connect(user='username', password='password', dsn=dsn_tns)

cursor = conn.cursor()
ddl_statement = "CREATE TABLE my_table(col1 INT, col2 VARCHAR(50))"
cursor.execute(ddl_statement)

cursor.close()
conn.close()

Here, a DSN (data source name) is created using the makedsn function, and a connection to the database is established using the connect function. Subsequently, a table named my_table is created using a cursor.

SET SERVEROUTPUT ON;

DROP PROCEDURE test_sp_1;

CREATE PROCEDURE test_sp
AS
BEGIN
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Test works');
END;
/

CREATE PROCEDURE test_sp_1
AS
BEGIN
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Testing');
    test_sp;
END;
/

In the above code, we have created two stored procedures - test_sp and test_sp_1. The test_sp procedure will print “Test works” on the console, and the test_sp_1 procedure will print “Testing” on the console and will call the test_sp procedure.

SELECT nonstops.term, nonstops.lincat, nonstops.id, 
MIN(
(1-((LEAST(1,minusone.catimp / nonstops.catimp) + LEAST(1,minusone.catweb / nonstops.catweb))/2))*
(1-((LEAST(1,minusone.catimp / nonstops.catimp) + LEAST(1,minusone.catweb / nonstops.catweb))/2))*
(1-((LEAST(1,minusone.catimp / nonstops.catimp) + LEAST(1,minusone.catweb / nonstops.catweb))/2))*

)
AS calc FROM nonstops INNER JOIN EACH minusone ON nonstops.lincat = minusone.lincat AND nonstops.term = minusone.term

CAST and CONVERT CAST and CONVERT functions are used to change data types of values. These two functions are commonly used in SQL Server, but they have some differences. CAST is a standard ANSI-SQL function that is used to convert an expression of one data type to another. It’s more limited compared to CONVERT because it doesn’t have a style parameter. CONVERT is a SQL Server-specific function that is used to convert an expression from one data type to another. One of its benefits over CAST is that it provides a style parameter that formats dates and times.

-- Concatenate strings with padding
SELECT printf('%-10s | %-15s', column1, column2) AS padded_result
FROM your_table;

item.title: Converting Comma-Separated String to Array in PL/SQL ORACLE SQL
item.description:
In PL/SQL, there are various approaches to convert a comma-separated string to an array. Two common methods involve using the built-in function DBMS_UTILITY.COMMA_TO_TABLE and employing XMLTABLE for conversion.

Using DBMS_UTILITY.COMMA_TO_TABLE

The built-in function DBMS_UTILITY.COMMA_TO_TABLE can be utilized for converting a comma-separated string to an array. However, it’s important to note that this function doesn’t work with numbers, requiring a workaround to ensure proper functionality.

DECLARE
  l_input VARCHAR2(4000) := '1,2,3';
  l_count BINARY_INTEGER;
  l_array DBMS_UTILITY.LNAME_ARRAY;
BEGIN
  DBMS_UTILITY.COMMA_TO_TABLE(
    list   => REGEXP_REPLACE(l_input, '(^|,)', '\1x'),
    tablen => l_count,
    tab    => l_array
  );
  DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(l_count);
  FOR i IN 1 .. l_count LOOP
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(
      'Element ' || TO_CHAR(i) || 
      ' of array contains: ' || 
      SUBSTR(l_array(i), 2)
    );
  END LOOP;
END;
/

To convert from hexadecimal to decimal in Oracle SQL, you can use the TO_NUMBER function with the format mask ‘xx’, as shown below:

SELECT TO_NUMBER('AA', 'xx') FROM DUAL; -- Returns 170

				  Here, 'AA' is the hexadecimal value to be converted. The 'xx' format mask tells Oracle to interpret the input as a hexadecimal value.  To convert from decimal to hexadecimal, you can use the TO\_CHAR function with the format mask 'xxxx', as shown below:  
				  

SELECT TO_CHAR(170, 'xxxx') FROM DUAL; -- Returns AA

Thread : Crashed: NSOperationQueue 0x170239c20 :: NSOperation 0x17024d7d0 (QOS: LEGACY)
0  libobjc.A.dylib                0x000000019701c0b4 objc_retain + 20

Answer by (Admin):

Amazon SNS vs Amazon SQS are both messaging services provided by Amazon Web Services (AWS). However, they are designed for different use cases and have some key differences.

Way to differentiate between Amazon SNS vs Amazon SQS:

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) is a push-based delivery system that uses a publish-subscribe model to send messages to subscribed endpoints or clients, while Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) is a pull-based delivery system that uses a queue-based system to store and retrieve messages between distributed application components.

item.title: Discovering Duplicate Rows In Sql Server
item.description:
Discovering Duplicate Rows in SQL Server In this blog post, we will explore how to find duplicate rows in SQL Server and retrieve the associated IDs of those rows. We will use the example of a database of organizations, where we want to remove duplicate organizations but still maintain the link to any associated users.

First, let’s start by running a query to find the duplicate organizations:

SELECT     orgName, COUNT(*) AS dupes  
FROM         organizations  
GROUP BY orgName  
HAVING      (COUNT(*) > 1)

				  This query will return the names of the duplicate organizations and the number of occurrences of each. Although, we also want to retrieve the IDs associated with each organization. We can do this by joining the original table with a subquery that returns the duplicate organizations and their counts:  
				  

SELECT o.orgName, oc.dupeCount, o.id
FROM organizations o
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT orgName, COUNT(*) AS dupeCount
    FROM organizations
    GROUP BY orgName
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
) oc ON o.orgName = oc.orgName

In this query, we join the original organizations table with a subquery that returns the duplicate organizations and their counts. We use an inner join to only retrieve the records that have a matching organization name in both the subquery and the original table. By including the ID column in the select statement, we can retrieve the IDs associated with each organization. If we want to delete the duplicate organizations, we can use the following query:

  • Views referencing the dropped column are invalidated, but not dropped. They will remain invalid until they are revised to work with the modified schema.
  • Stored procedures referencing the dropped column are also invalidated.
  • The column ID numbers of following columns are reset.
  • Permissions granted specifically on the dropped column will be removed.
  • Indexes referencing the dropped column are dropped as well.

Problem Description

A common error encountered when querying an Oracle Database is the “specified field not found in datetime or interval” error. This error typically arises when performing comparison operations involving timestamps with intervals. An example of this type of query is:

SELECT * 
FROM MY_TABLE T
WHERE T.MY_TIMESTAMP >= (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '1' HOUR );

In the above example, we are selecting rows from the “MY_TABLE” table where “MY_TIMESTAMP” is greater than or equal to the timestamp value of one hour ago. The error occurs when the specified field is not found in the datetime or interval, commonly due to differences in timezone/DST settings.

item.description:
Efficient Base64 Encoding and Decoding in Oracle

Base64 Encoding and Decoding in Oracle

If you need to encode or decode a value in Base64 format in Oracle, you can use the UTL_ENCODE.BASE64_ENCODE and UTL_ENCODE.BASE64_DECODE functions.

Encoding a Value in Base64

To encode a value in Base64 format, you can use the following code:

function to_base64(t in varchar2) return varchar2 is
begin
  return utl_raw.cast_to_varchar2(
    utl_encode.base64_encode(utl_raw.cast_to_raw(t))
  );
end to_base64;

Here, the input value t is first cast to a raw value, which is then encoded in Base64 format using the UTL_ENCODE.BASE64_ENCODE function. The resulting raw value is then cast back to a varchar2 value using the UTL_RAW.CAST_TO_VARCHAR2 function.

item.title: Efficient Oracle Sql Insertions With With Clause
item.description:
Efficient Oracle SQL Insertions with WITH Clause Inserting data into a table is a common operation in SQL, and the WITH clause is used to define a temporary table that can be referenced within the SQL statement. In this case, the temporary table is called “helper_table”.

Here is an example of using WITH clause with INSERT INTO:

INSERT INTO dummy1
 WITH helper_table AS (
   SELECT *
   FROM dummy2
 )
 SELECT t.a
 FROM helper_table t
 WHERE t.a="X";

				   This query inserts data into the "dummy1" table from the "helper\_table" defined in the WITH clause. The SELECT statement within the INSERT INTO statement defines what data is inserted into "dummy1".   If you have multiple helper tables, you can include them in the WITH clause like this:  
				  

INSERT INTO dummy
 WITH helper_table AS (
   SELECT *
   FROM dummy2
 ),
 helper_table2 AS (
   SELECT *
   FROM dummy3
 )
 SELECT t.value as a, t2.value as b
 FROM helper_table t 
 JOIN helper_table t2 ON t.value = t2.value
 WHERE t.value="X" AND t2.value="X";

In this example, data is inserted into “dummy” table from the “helper_table” and “helper_table2”. The JOIN statement combines the two tables and the WHERE clause limits the results to only include values where “value” is “X” in both tables. It’s important to note that the syntax of WITH clause with INSERT INTO may vary depending on the SQL database being used. As an alternative, you could use a subquery instead of a WITH clause like this:

item.title: Efficiently Calculating Median In Google Bigquery A Guide
item.description:
Calculating Median of a Numeric Sequence in Google BigQuery
If you need to calculate the median value of a numeric sequence in Google BigQuery efficiently, you can use the PERCENTILE_CONT window function, which returns values that are based on linear interpolation between the values of the group, ordering them per the ORDER BY clause.

PERCENTILE_CONT Syntax

The syntax for PERCENTILE_CONT function is:

PERCENTILE_CONT(numeric-expression) 
WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY column ASC|DESC) OVER (
    [PARTITION BY partition-expression, ... ]
    [ORDER BY column-expression, ... [ASC|DESC], ... ]
    [framespec]
)

numeric-expression - A numeric expression for which you want to calculate the percentile.
column - A column indicating the order for calculation of percentile.
partition-expression - Defines the partition criteria for the percentile calculation.
framespec - Defines a window over which percentile is to be computed.

item.title: Exploring Oracle Sequence Transactionality
item.description:
Exploring Oracle Sequence Transactionality Oracle Sequence Transactionality
One common scenario in Oracle databases is the need to assign a unique number to a field on an entity. This unique number could be used as a primary key or a different field. One of the ways to generate this number is by creating a sequence.

Creating a Sequence

Here’s an example of creating a sequence in Oracle:

CREATE SEQUENCE MySequence
  MINVALUE 65536 
  MAXVALUE 4294967296 
  START WITH 65536
  INCREMENT BY 1
  CYCLE
  NOCACHE
  ORDER;

In this example, we’re creating a sequence called “MySequence” with a minimum value of 65536 and a maximum value of 4294967296. It starts at 65536 and increments by 1 each time. We’re also telling Oracle to cycle back to the minimum value when it reaches the maximum value and not to cache numbers in memory for performance reasons.

SELECT TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(1230219000000)     # 2008-12-25 15:30:00 UTC
SELECT DATE(TIMESTAMP(1424184621000000))   # 2015-02-17 
SELECT DATE(TIMESTAMP('2015-02-17'))       # 2015-02-17

item.description:
Determining the size of your MySQL database is crucial for managing storage and optimizing performance. This article provides insights into calculating the size of your MySQL database using SQL queries and tools.

1. Using SQL Queries:

Calculate Total Database Size:

You can use the following query to calculate the total size of your MySQL database:

SELECT
    table_schema AS "Database",
    SUM(data_length + index_length) / (1024 * 1024) AS "Size (MB)"
FROM information_schema.tables
GROUP BY table_schema;

This query retrieves the data and index lengths of each table in the database, summing them up to provide the total size in megabytes.

item.description:
Finding Current Open Cursors in Oracle: A Guide How to Find Current Open Cursors in Oracle

To find the number of current open cursors in an Oracle instance, you can use the following queries:

  1. Total Cursors Open, By Session: This query provides the total number of opened cursors for each session.
SELECT a.value, s.username, s.sid, s.serial#
FROM v$sesstat a, v$statname b, v$session s
WHERE a.statistic# = b.statistic#  AND s.sid=a.sid
AND b.name="opened cursors current";

Here, we are selecting values for opened cursors, username, session id, and serial number from v$sesstat, v$statname, and v$session tables. The accuracy of this data is based on pseudo-tables (“x$” tables) that point directly to the relevant portions of the SGA; hence you cannot get more accurate than that.

item.title: Finding Duplicate Values In Oracle Table
item.description:
Finding Duplicate Values in Oracle Table : Explained with SQL Code
If you are working with an Oracle database, you may need to find the duplicate values in a table. In such a scenario, you can use SQL queries to find the duplicate values in the table.

Finding Duplicate Values with SQL Query

To find the duplicate values in a table, you can use the following SQL query:

SELECT column_name, COUNT(column_name)
FROM table_name
GROUP BY column_name
HAVING COUNT(column_name) > 1;

Here, replace column_name with the name of the column whose duplicate values you want to find and table_name with the name of the table. This query aggregates the column by COUNT, and then uses a HAVING clause to find values that appear more than once.

SELECT
  FK.OWNER||'.'||FK.TABLE_NAME AS CHILD_TABLE,
  SRC.OWNER||'.'||SRC.TABLE_NAME AS PARENT_TABLE,
  FK.CONSTRAINT_NAME AS FK_CONSTRAINT,
  SRC.CONSTRAINT_NAME AS REFERENCED_CONSTRAINT
FROM ALL_CONSTRAINTS FK
JOIN ALL_CONSTRAINTS SRC ON FK.R_CONSTRAINT_NAME = SRC.CONSTRAINT_NAME
WHERE
  FK.CONSTRAINT_TYPE = 'R'
  AND SRC.OWNER = 'MY_SCHEMA'
  AND SRC.TABLE_NAME = 'MY_TABLE';

item.title: Fixing Invalid Oracle Url Error With Oracledatasourcemakeurl
item.description:
Fixing Invalid Oracle URL Error with OracleDataSourcemakeURL Connecting to a local Oracle database can be frustrating, especially when cryptic error messages like “Invalid Oracle URL specified: OracleDataSource.makeURL” pop up. In this post, we’ll explore how to troubleshoot this error and connect to the database successfully.

First, let’s take a look at the code used for connecting to the database:

OracleDataSource dataSource = new OracleDataSource();
 dataSource.setServerName("localhost");
 dataSource.setUser(userName);
 dataSource.setPassword(password);
 dataSource.setDatabaseName("orcl");
 return dataSource.getConnection();

				  This code creates a new instance of the OracleDataSource class and sets the server name, username, password, and database name for the connection. Although, this code alone may not work for every installation of Oracle.   If you're encountering the "Invalid Oracle URL specified: OracleDataSource.makeURL" error, it's likely due to incorrect connection parameters. One common mistake is not using the correct URL syntax. The correct format for the URL is "jdbc:oracle:thin:@hostname:port:SID" or "jdbc:oracle:thin:@hostname:port/service\_name".   If you're using setURL or your container is doing it for you, make sure you use the correct syntax, with a colon before "@". The datasource class tries to parse the URL and gives a cryptic error message if there are syntax issues.   Along with using the correct URL syntax, you may also need to set the port number and driver type for the connection. Adding the following two lines of code to the original code can solve the problem:  
				  

dataSource.setPortNumber(1521);
 dataSource.setDriverType("thin");

It’s important to note that these additional parameters may not have been needed in previous installations of Oracle, but may be required for your specific setup. The error message does not provide much detail, so it’s important to check all connection parameters and syntax to ensure they are correct. For WildFly users, you may need to add additional parameters for the DataSource. Navigate to DataSource -> Connection -> Connection Properties and add “driverType=thin” to the parameters. Double-check that you are using the correct DataSource type as well (in some cases, using an XA DataSource can solve the problem). In summary, when encountering the “Invalid Oracle URL specified: OracleDataSource.makeURL” error message, it’s important to double-check your connection parameters and ensure you’re using the correct URL syntax. Adding additional parameters like port number and driver type may also be necessary for successful database connectivity. By taking these steps, you can troubleshoot the error and successfully connect to your local Oracle database.]]>

item.title: Formatting Date As Mm Dd Yyyy In Google Bigquery Query Results
item.description:
How to format date as mm/dd/yyyy in Google BigQuery SQL?

Summary

To format a date as mm/dd/yyyy in Google BigQuery SQL, you can use either the STRFTIME_UTC_USEC function in Legacy SQL or the FORMAT_DATE function in Standard SQL.

Using STRFTIME_UTC_USEC function in Legacy SQL

To format a date as mm/dd/yyyy in Legacy SQL, use the STRFTIME_UTC_USEC function with the date value and the desired format string. For example:

SELECT 
  STRFTIME_UTC_USEC("2016-10-20", "%m/%d/%Y"),   
  STRFTIME_UTC_USEC(CURRENT_DATE(), "%m/%d/%Y")

In this query, the first line formats the date “2016-10-20” as “10/20/2016”, and the second line formats the current date as mm/dd/yyyy format. The %m, %d, and %Y are format codes for month, day, and year respectively.

item.title: Generating Random Uuids On Oracle A Quick Guide
item.description:
Generating Random UUIDs on Oracle: A Quick Guide How to generate a random UUID in Oracle using SYS_GUID

If you’re unable to use Java in your Oracle environment, another option is to generate a random number and convert it to a UUID format. Here’s an example of how to do that:

-- Generate random number (between 0 and 2^32-1)
WITH random_num AS (
    SELECT DBMS_RANDOM.VALUE(0, POWER(2, 32) - 1) AS num
    FROM dual
)
-- Convert random number to UUID format
SELECT 
    TO_CHAR(UPPER(HEXTORAW(RPAD(RPAD(LTRIM(TO_CHAR(num, 'XXXXXX')), 8, '0'), 32, '0'))), 'XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX') AS random_uuid
FROM random_num;

This approach converts a randomly generated number into a UUID format following the guidelines in RFC 4122 . Although, note that this approach may not be as reliable as using a Java function or SYS_GUID. Also note that performance-wise, generating a random number and converting it to a UUID format may be slower than using SYS_GUID or a Java function.]]>

item.title: Google Bigquery Amazon Redshift Column Based Relational Or Nosql Database
item.description:
Learning Column-based Databases and Google BigQuery/Amazon Redshift

What are Column-based Databases?

Column-based databases store data in columns instead of rows making it easier and more efficient to access data. Unlike traditional row-based databases, which store data sequentially in rows, column-based databases store data in a columnar format based on data type.

Column-based Relational Databases vs Column-based NoSQL Databases

Column-based relational databases, such as InfoBright, Vertica, and Sybase IQ, are based on the structured query language (SQL) and provide support for transactions, tables, and indexes. On the other hand, column-based NoSQL databases, such as Cassandra and HBase, are designed to handle unstructured and semi-structured data and do not provide support for transactions, tables, and indexes. They use a distributed database architecture optimized for scalability and high performance.

item.title: Google Bigquery Authenticating Google Api Using Java Api A Service Account
item.description:
Authenticating Google API with a service account with Java API

Summary

In this post, we will learn how to authenticate a Google service account through the Java API and access Google Bigquery. We will provide a code example and explain each line of code.

Code Example

 /** Global instance of the HTTP transport. */
 private static final HttpTransport HTTP_TRANSPORT = new NetHttpTransport();

 /** Global instance of the JSON factory. */
 private static final JsonFactory JSON_FACTORY = new JacksonFactory();

 private static Bigquery bigquery;

 public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    GoogleCredential credential = new GoogleCredential.Builder().setTransport(HTTP_TRANSPORT)
        .setJsonFactory(JSON_FACTORY)
        .setServiceAccountId(SERVICE_ACCOUNT_EMAIL)
        .setServiceAccountScopes(BigqueryScopes.BIGQUERY)
        .setServiceAccountPrivateKeyFromP12File(new File("path/to/privatekey.p12"))
        .build();

    bigquery = new Bigquery.Builder(HTTP_TRANSPORT, JSON_FACTORY, credential)
       .setApplicationName(APP_NAME)
       .build();

    listDatasets(bigquery, "publicdata");
}

 private static void listDatasets(Bigquery bigquery, String projectId) throws IOException {
    Datasets.List datasetRequest = bigquery.datasets().list(projectId);
    DatasetList datasets = datasetRequest.execute();
    System.out.println("Available datasetsn-");
    for (DatasetList.Datasets dataset : datasets.getDatasets()) {
        System.out.format("%sn", dataset.getDatasetReference().getDatasetId());
    }
}

If you are trying to sort data in Big Query by applying a case when statement in the order by clause, you may have noticed that it doesn’t work, even though it may have worked in other SQL environments. In this post, we will explore whether or not Big Query supports custom sorting and provide practical examples to help clarify the issue.

Learning the ORDER BY clause

Before we dive into Big Query’s capabilities, let’s first take a look at the ORDER BY clause in SQL. The ORDER BY clause sorts the results of a query in ascending or descending order of one or more fields. You can sort by field names or by aliases from the SELECT clause. To sort by multiple fields or aliases, enter them as a comma-separated list. The results are sorted on the fields in the order in which they are listed.

item.title: Google Bigquery Bigquery Correlation Multi Column Utilization
item.description:
Introduction:

In this post, we will discuss how to use BigQuery CORR() to find the correlation between the rows of a dataset with 100k rows and 100 columns. We will provide step-by-step instructions with code to help you know how the process works.

Schema:

The schema of the dataset is as follows:

id: integer, feature1: float, feature2: float, ..., feature100: float

				  The goal is to find the correlation between the rows based on the 100 features.    Step-by-Step Instructions:  1. To use BigQuery CORR(), we must first create a table with the dataset. We can do that by uploading the dataset to Google Cloud Storage or by importing it directly to BigQuery.  2. Once we have created the table, we can use the following query to find the correlation between each column and the other columns:     
				  

SELECT CORR(col1, col2), CORR(col1, col3), CORR(col1, col4), ..., CORR(col99, col100)
   FROM [mytable]

				
We must replace "mytable" with the name of our table.     This query will take a significant amount of time to execute, and it will be challenging to automate. Therefore, we must consider an alternative approach.   3. One possible solution is to transform the table so that everything lives in three columns: colname, value, and rowid. We can do that with the following query:     
				  

SELECT colname, value, rowid FROM
   (SELECT 'col1' AS colname, col1, rowid AS value FROM [mytable]),
   (SELECT 'col2' AS colname, col2, rowid AS value FROM [mytable]),
   (SELECT 'col3' AS colname, col3, rowid AS value FROM [mytable]),
   ...
   (SELECT 'col100' AS colname, col100 AS value FROM [mytable])

				
In this query, we create a subquery for each column, where we select the column name as "colname," the column value as "value," and the row ID as "rowid." We then merge all these subqueries using the UNION operator.     This query will create a new table with three columns: colname, value, and rowid. The colname column will contain the name of each column, the value column will hold the value of each feature for each row, and the rowid column will store the ID of each row.     This new table will make it easier to find the correlation between the rows based on the 100 features.    4. Now we can run the following query to find the correlation between the rows:     
				  

SELECT CORR(a.value, b.value) corr, a.colname, b.colname
   FROM [my_new_table] a
   JOIN EACH [my_new_table] b
   ON a.rowid=b.rowid
   WHERE a.colname>b.colname
   GROUP BY a.colname, b.colname

				
We must replace "my\_new\_table" with the name of the new table that we created in step 3.     In this query, we join the new table with itself based on the rowid column, so we can compare the values of each feature for each row.     We then use the WHERE clause to ensure that we only compare different column names (i.e., we do not find the correlation between the same columns).     Lastly, we group the results by column names to get the correlation between the rows based on the 100 features.   Summary:  To use BigQuery CORR() to find the correlation between the rows of a dataset with 100k rows and 100 columns, we must create a new table with three columns: colname, value, and rowid. We can then use a query to join this new table with itself and find the correlation between the values of each feature for each row.   Alternative Ways:  An alternative way to find the correlation between the rows is to use a Python script and the Pandas library. Pandas provides a corr() function that can calculate the correlation coefficients for all possible pairs of columns in a dataset.  We can use]]>

item.title: Google Bigquery Bigquery Incompatible Types In Union All
item.description:
Summary: The error occurs because there is a mismatch in the data type of the DebugData field in the two tables. The solution is to cast the DebugData field in the RawGPS table as a string using the CAST function.

Code Explanation: The code uses Common Table Expression (CTE) to simplify the queries and make them more readable.

  • The RawDebug CTE selects the DebugReason and DebugData fields as a named struct from the Debug table with a table wildcard to include data from multiple tables.
  • The RawGPS CTE uses the same struct format for the Debug field, but because there is no field with such name in GPS table, null values are used instead.
  • The final SELECT statement uses UNION ALL to combine the two tables horizontally. Although, since the DebugData field has different data types, an error occurs.

To fix it, we need to cast the DebugData field in the RawGPS table as a string using the CAST function. We add the line CAST(DebugData AS STRING) AS DebugData to the RawGPS table, and it converts the DebugData field to a string.

item.title: Google Bigquery Bigquery Introduces New Pricing Tiers
item.description:

The BigQuery pricing model is set to change on January 1st, 2016, and a new tiered pricing model will be introduced. To help customers predict cost implications, the JSON response can be used to see what tier has been assigned to a query and analyze potential costs.

What is the ‘billingTier’ field in BigQuery?

The ‘billingTier’ field in the BigQuery JSON response is a true indicator of the tier assigned to a query according to the upcoming pricing structure. If the field is set to 1 in the response, then the query would be billed at the current (tier 1) rates under the new pricing structure.

Although, when data is streamed into BigQuery, it doesn’t immediately become part of the permanent storage - instead, it is stored in a temporary buffer called the ‘streaming buffer’. The streaming buffer is an essential part of BigQuery’s streaming functionality, but it can cause issues when trying to update or modify existing data. In this post, we will explore the streaming output buffer in BigQuery, and how it affects updating partitioned tables. We will also provide some practical examples to demonstrate how to work with partitioned tables in BigQuery.

What are Clusters?

Clusters allow you to organize your tables based on the values of one or more columns. The clustered column(s) are used to physically sort the data, which allows for faster queries that utilize the same column(s). Essentially, clusters improve query performance by reducing the amount of data that needs to be scanned.

What is Transaction Isolation Level?

Transaction isolation level refers to the degree to which one transaction must be isolated from other transactions while accessing the database. This means that if multiple transactions are executing concurrently, they must be isolated from each other to ensure data consistency and integrity.

What is row-level expiration in BigQuery?

Row-level expiration in BigQuery is the ability to set an expiration time on individual rows in a table. With row-level expiration, you can specify that a row should be deleted automatically after a certain period of time has elapsed. This is useful for scenarios where you have data that is only relevant for a specific period of time, such as session data or logs.

item.title: Google Bigquery Calculating Session Session Duration In Firebase Analytics Raw Data A Guide
item.description:
Summary: The Firebase Analytics raw data linked to BigQuery can be used to calculate Session and Session duration. To define a session, we can use a query that breaks sessions whenever a user is inactive for more than 20 minutes. We can then use a trick to find all sessions with SQL.

To calculate the session duration, we can use the following SQL query:

#standardSQL

SELECT app_instance_id, sess_id, MIN(min_time) sess_start, MAX(max_time) sess_end, COUNT() records, MAX(sess_id) OVER(PARTITION BY app_instance_id) total_sessions, (ROUND((MAX(max_time)-MIN(min_time))/(10001000),1)) sess_length_seconds FROM ( SELECT *, SUM(session_start) OVER(PARTITION BY app_instance_id ORDER BY event_timestamp) sess_id FROM ( SELECT *, IF(event_timestamp - LAG(event_timestamp, 1, 0) OVER(PARTITION BY app_instance_id ORDER BY event_timestamp) > 20 * 60 * 1000 * 1000, 1, 0) session_start FROM your_dataset.your_table_name ) ) GROUP BY app_instance_id, sess_id In this query, we first use a subquery to mark the start of each session if there has been an inactive period of 20 minutes or more. We then use another subquery to assign a session ID to each event based on the session start marker. Lastly, we group by app_instance_id and sess_id to calculate the session start and end times, the number of records in each session, and the session length in seconds. Alternative Ways: Another approach to calculate session duration is to use the session_start and session_end events that Firebase Analytics automatically logs. These events mark the start and end of each session, and their parameters include the session length. We can extract this data using a SQL query like the following: #standardSQL SELECT app_instance_id, event_date, user_first_touch_timestamp, event_timestamp, (SELECT value.int_value FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = ‘firebase_event_origin’) event_origin, (SELECT value.int_value FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = ‘session_length’) session_length_seconds FROM your_dataset.your_table_name WHERE (SELECT value.string_value FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = ‘firebase_event_origin’) IN (‘session_start’, ‘session_end’) This query extracts the session_start and session_end events and their parameters, including the session length. We can then join the session_start and session_end events with a common session ID to calculate the session start and end times, the number of records in each session, and the session length in seconds. Practical Examples: Suppose we have a mobile app that tracks user activity using Firebase Analytics, and we want to analyze user sessions by country and time. We can use the following SQL query to calculate the session duration by country and hour: #standardSQL SELECT event_date, FORMAT_TIMESTAMP(’%Y-%m-%d %H:00:00’, TIMESTAMP_MICROS(event_timestamp)) AS hour, (SELECT value.string_value FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = ‘geo’) AS country, SUM( IF( (event_timestamp - LAG(event_timestamp, 1, 0) OVER(PARTITION BY app_instance_id ORDER BY event_timestamp) > 20 * 60 * 1000 * 1000), 0, (event_timestamp - LAG(event_timestamp, 1, 0) OVER(PARTITION BY app_instance_id ORDER BY event_timestamp)) ) ) / 1000000 AS session_length_seconds FROM your_dataset.your_table_name WHERE event_name = ‘screen_view’ AND EXISTS (SELECT * FROM UNNEST(event_params) WHERE key = ‘geo’) GROUP BY event_date, hour, country ORDER BY event_date, hour, country This query uses a subquery to extract the country from the geo parameter, and then groups by event_date, hour, and country to calculate the session length in seconds. The calculation uses a nested IF function to exclude inactive periods of 20 minutes or more. References: 1. https://firebase.google.com/docs/analytics/export/bigquery 2. https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference]]>

Causes of “resources exceeded” Error

The most common reasons for this error message are:

1. Skewed Data

When your data is heavily skewed towards one key value, one worker task can end up with most of the records, which creates an overload. For instance, if you have millions of records, but only a few are associated with one particular user ID, this can produce a skewed dataset. As a result, BigQuery workers can’t distribute the load equally, and “resources exceeded” error occurs.

Problem:

You want to convert a JSON file into newline delimited JSON format in Python so that it can be uploaded from Cloud Storage into BigQuery.

Solution:

You can use the built-in json module to achieve this. Here is a sample code:

import json

# open the JSON file
with open('input.json', 'r') as f:
    # load the JSON records into a list
    records = json.load(f)

# convert the records to newline delimited JSON format
ndjson = 'n'.join([json.dumps(record) for record in records])

# write the newline delimited JSON to a file
with open('output.ndjson', 'w') as f:
    f.write(ndjson)

The json.load() method loads the JSON records from the input file into a list of dictionaries. Then, we use a list comprehension to convert each dictionary to a JSON string using json.dumps(). Lastly, we join the JSON strings with newline characters and write the result to an output file.

item.title: Google Bigquery Converting Timestamp To Seconds In Bigquery Standard Sql
item.description:
Converting Timestamp to Seconds in BigQuery Standard SQL
In BigQuery Standard SQL, we can use the UNIX_SECONDS() function to convert a timestamp to seconds. This function returns the UNIX timestamp in seconds, which counts the number of seconds since January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC.

Converting Current Timestamp to Seconds

Let’s consider an example of converting the current timestamp to seconds using the UNIX_SECONDS() function in BigQuery Standard SQL:

SELECT UNIX_SECONDS(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) AS current_timestamp_in_seconds

In the above code, we are selecting the current timestamp using the CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() function, and then using the UNIX_SECONDS() function to convert it to seconds. We are also giving an alias current_timestamp_in_seconds to the result column.

item.title: Google Bigquery Coping With Changing Schemas
item.description:
Dealing with Evolving Schemas in BigQuery

Problem Statement

We are a gaming company that stores events to BigQuery. We store up to 1 giga events per day and shard them over month and application in order to lower query costs. Our current solution supports adding new types of events which leads to new versions of the table schema. These new schemas are denoted by the version number and the month in which they were added, i.e., events_app1_v2_201308 and events_app1_v2_201308. If we add events with new column types in September we will also get events_app1_v3_201309. We have written code that finds out the involved tables (for a date range) and makes a union of them using BigQuery’s comma-separated FROM clause. Although, we just realized that this will not work when we make unions over different versions of the event tables. Our problem is how to deal with evolving schemas in BigQuery.

item.title: Google Bigquery Counting Element Frequency In Bigquery Array Field A How To Guide
item.description: Objective: Count frequency of elements in a BigQuery array field Table structure: The table has four columns - author_id, year, and three columns l_0, l_1, and l_2, that contain an array of strings. Desired output: A table that gives a frequency count of the elements in the fields l_0, l_1, and l_2. Assumptions: The desired output is on a per-array basis. Solution: One way to achieve the desired output is to use the UNNEST function to flatten the array fields and then count the frequency of each element. We can then use the ANY_VALUE function to group the remaining columns. The following query demonstrates this approach: SELECT author_id, year, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_0 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_0) AS l_0 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_0, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_1 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_1) AS l_1 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_1, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_2 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_2) AS l_2 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_2 FROM my_table GROUP BY author_id, year Let’s break down the code line by line: - The first part of the query is the column selection for author_id and year. SELECT author_id, year, - We then determine the frequency of elements in the l_0 array using the UNNEST function to flatten it and counting the frequency of each element using the COUNT function. We can then use ARRAY_AGG function to collect the counts and names into an array of structs. (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_0 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_0) AS l_0 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_0, - The same approach is repeated for the l_1 and l_2 arrays. (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_1 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_1) AS l_1 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_1, (SELECT ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(name, count)) FROM ( SELECT l_2 AS name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM UNNEST(l_2) AS l_2 GROUP BY 1 ) ) AS l_2 - Lastly, we group our results by author_id and year. FROM my_table GROUP BY author_id, year Alternative ways: Another approach to count the frequency of elements in a BigQuery array field is to use the STRUCT and UNNEST functions to flatten the array and then aggregate the results using GROUP BY. Here is an example: ``` SELECT author_id, year, ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(l_0.name AS name, l_0.count AS count)) AS l_0, ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(l_1.name AS name, l_1.count AS count)) AS l_1, ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(l_2.name AS name, l_2.count AS count)) AS l_2 FROM ( SELECT author_id, year, name, COUNT(*) AS count FROM my_table, UNNEST(l_0) AS name GROUP BY author_id, year, name ) l_0 FULL OUTER JOIN ( SELECT]]>

item.title: Google Bigquery Creating A Partitioned Table In Bigquery
item.description:
Creating Partitioned Tables in BigQuery In March 2016, Google announced partitioned tables feature in BigQuery that offers significant advantages.
Creating a partitioned table in BigQuery could be done using the UI, the CLI, or the API.

Creating Partitioned Table in BigQuery through CLI

To create a partitioned table using the CLI, run the following command:

bq query --use_legacy_sql=false '
CREATE TABLE [DATASET].[TABLENAME] (
    [COLUMN] [DATATYPE],
    ...
    [COLUMN] [DATATYPE],
    [PARTITION_COLUMN] DATE)
PARTITION BY [PARTITION_COLUMN]
OPTIONS(
  expiration_timestamp=TIMESTAMP "2028-01-01 00:00:00 UTC",
  description="Example partitioned table create in BQ CLI",
  labels=[("partition","summary")]
);'

The command above creates a table with the given table name and dataset name in BigQuery. The table schema contains one or more columns defined by column_name and data_type.
The partition column is defined by the column name on which you want to partition the table. Here, the date column is chosen for partitioning.
The OPTIONS parameter sets the expiration date for the table, adds description, and sets labels.

item.title: Google Bigquery Differentiating Totalbytesbilled Totalbytesprocessed
item.description:
Learning totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed in BigQuery

What are totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed?

totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed are statistics provided by Google BigQuery that track the amount of data processed and billed for a particular query or job. Here, “processed” refers to the amount of data that was actually read and used by the query, while “billed” refers to the amount of data that was reserved in advance to execute the query.

What is the difference between totalBytesBilled and totalBytesProcessed?

totalBytesProcessed refers to the amount of data read and processed by BigQuery to execute the query. This includes data that was read from storage, as well as any intermediate data created during the query execution. totalBytesBilled, on the other hand, refers to the amount of data reserved by BigQuery for the query in advance. This includes data that may have been filtered out before it was processed, as well as any data that was read but ultimately not used in the query. As a result, it is possible for totalBytesBilled to be higher than totalBytesProcessed, particularly for small queries that are run on heavily constrained systems where BigQuery needs to reserve resources in advance to ensure that the query completes quickly.

The first method involves using the DATE() and TIMESTAMP_MILLIS() functions. Here’s how:

# standardSQL query
SELECT DATE(TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(CAST((timestamp) AS INT64))) AS date
FROM YourTable;

In the above query:

  • The TIMESTAMP_MILLIS() function is used to convert timestamp to milliseconds.

item.title: Google Bigquery Error In Apache Beam Bigquery Streaming Insert Runtimeexception With Managedchannel Allocation Site
item.description:
Apache Beam - Bigquery streaming insert RuntimeException

Summary

While running a streaming Apache Beam pipeline in Google Dataflow, which reads data from Kafka and streams inserts to Bigquery, a large number of warnings were thrown during the Bigquery streaming insert step. The error message reads “java.lang.RuntimeException: ManagedChannel allocation site”.

Explanation

The error message suggests that the issue is related to the gRPC channel provided by Google’s API Gateway. These errors occur when there is an issue with the creation or allocation of channels in gRPC, which could happen due to various reasons including network connectivity issues or resource constraints. In this specific case, the issue could be related to the fact that the pipeline is attempting to insert data into Bigquery at a higher rate than the channel can handle. It is also possible that the Dataflow VMs running the pipeline may have reached their network bandwidth limits. The error message suggests that the issue is related to the creation of the ManagedChannel, which is established by the InstantiatingGrpcChannelProvider. When creating a Bigquery client, the method first creates a ChannelPool and then a channel for every stream. In this process, if any of the channels created fail, the error message may occur.

item.description:
BigQuery executing only one query

Summary:

In BigQuery, while running a query in the UI, if you get the error “Error: 6.1 - 0.0: Only one query can be executed at a time,” it means that the query string has been parsed as containing multiple queries. This error occurs when there are multiple top-level SELECT statements in the query text box.

Explanation:

When running a query in BigQuery, you can only execute one query at a time. This means that you cannot have multiple top-level SELECT statements in the query text box. The error message “Error: 6.1 - 0.0: Only one query can be executed at a time” indicates that the query string has been parsed as containing multiple queries. The second query may be beginning on or around line 6. To fix this error, check the query text box to ensure that there are no multiple top-level SELECT statements. If there are, remove them or split them into separate queries.

SELECT word, nextword, COUNT(*) c

SELECT pos, title, word, LEAD(word) OVER(PARTITION BY created_utc,title ORDER BY pos) nextword FROM (
SELECT created_utc, title, word, pos FROM FLATTEN(
  (SELECT created_utc, title, SPLIT(title, ' ') word FROM [bigquery-samples:reddit.full])
  ), word)
))
WHERE nextword IS NOT null
GROUP EACH BY 1, 2
ORDER BY c DESC
LIMIT 100

Learning the Error

The error “Field payload.pages from table publicdata:samples.github_nested is not a leaf field” means that the field you are trying to select is a nested field and not a leaf field. A leaf field is a field that does not contain any other fields. In contrast, a nested field is a field that contains one or more fields. In BigQuery, you can only select leaf fields, so you need to flatten the nested field before you can select it.

from google.cloud import bigquery
def my_update_function(context,data):
    BQ = bigquery.Client()
    query_job = BQ.query("Update table set etc...")
    rows = query_job.result()
    return(rows)

The code imports the BigQuery client library from the google.cloud package and creates a function named my_update_function that takes two arguments: context and data. The function creates a BigQuery client object and stores it in the BQ variable. Then, it creates a query_job object by calling the query method on BQ and passing a SQL query as an argument. The return statement returns the rows object to the caller.

Where Does BigQuery Store Data?

By default, BigQuery stores your data in two regions: us-central1 and us-central2. Although, you can specify where your BigQuery data gets stored. Currently, there are three possible values: US, EU, and unspecified. If you specify US, your data is stored in us-central1 and us-central2. If you specify EU, your data is stored in europe-west1. item.title: Google Bigquery How To Get First Record Of A Specific Column In Bigquery
item.description:
How to get the first record of a specific column in BigQuery?
If you want to get the first record of a specific column in BigQuery, you can use the hits.time column which represents the number of milliseconds after the visitStartTime when the hit was recorded. The first hit has a hits.time of 0, so you just have to query for hits.time=0.

Example:

SELECT 
  STRFTIME_UTC_USEC(date, '%U') AS WK, 
  visitId, 
  date AS SALES_DATE, 
  hits.eventInfo.eventLabel AS SEARCH_DD, 
  year(date) as yr, 
  hits.time AS t
FROM
  (TABLE_DATE_RANGE([67977396.ga_sessions_], TIMESTAMP('2015-03-04'), TIMESTAMP('2015-03-04')))
WHERE 
  hits.eventInfo.eventAction='Depart date' 
  AND hits.eventInfo.eventCategory='Book a train'
  AND hits.time=0
ORDER BY 
  visitId

The query above selects the first record of the hits.time column for each visitId. It retrieves the week number, visitId, date, eventLabel, year and hits.time column. The results are filtered by the specified conditions, and ordered by visitId.

item.title: Google Bigquery How To Get Table Schema Using Python Bigquery Api
item.description:
Python BigQuery API - Get Table Schema BigQuery is a cloud-based data warehouse and storage solution provided by Google. In this post, we will be discussing how to fetch the schema of a table using the Python BigQuery API.

Dependencies

Before we begin, you need to install the following dependencies:

  • google-cloud-bigquery library
  • google-cloud-storage library

Code Explanation

The below code fetches the schema of a table in BigQuery:

from google.cloud import bigquery
from google.cloud import storage

# Creating BigQuery client object
client =  bigquery.Client.from_service_account_json('service_account.json')

def extract_table_schema(client): 
    # Setting up BigQuery dataset and table id
    project = "bigquery-public-data"
    dataset_id = 'samples'
    table_id = 'shakespeare'

    # Constructing BigQuery reference objects
    dataset_ref = client.dataset(dataset_id, project=project)
    table_ref = dataset_ref.table(table_id)
    
    # Fetching Table metadata
    table = client.get_table(table_ref) 

    # Parsing Table Schema
    schema = table.schema
    schema_list = []

    for field in schema:
        schema_list.append(field.name + ' ' + field.field_type)

    # Returning schema as string
    return ','.join(schema_list)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    table_schema = extract_table_schema(client)
    print(table_schema)

Code Breakdown

  • First, we import the necessary libraries - google.cloud.bigquery and google.cloud.storage
  • A BigQuery client object is created using the service account credentials stored in service_account.json
  • We define a function extract_table_schema that takes the BigQuery client object as input
  • Next, we define the project id, the dataset id, and the table id that we want to fetch schema from
  • We create BigQuery dataset and table reference objects using the client object and ids defined above
  • The get_table method of the client object is used to fetch metadata about the table
  • The schema of the table is accessed using the schema property of the table object
  • We iterate over the fields in the schema and add a string with the format fieldname fieldtype to a list
  • Lastly, the list is joined using commas and returned as a string

Code Output

The function returns the schema of the specified table as a comma-separated string with each field in the format fieldname fieldtype

In this code example, we are creating a BigQuery table with a complex schema using Python client. We will define the schema using the bigquery.SchemaField() function to define the fields of the table.

Code

from google.cloud import bigquery

# Create a BigQuery Client object
client = bigquery.Client()

# Define the schema fields for the table
schema = [
    bigquery.SchemaField('user', 'STRING'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('id', 'STRING'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('service_origin', 'STRING'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('name', 'STRING'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('mimeType', 'STRING'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('createdAt', 'DATETIME'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('ownedByMe', 'BOOLEAN'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('owners', 'ARRAY>', 'REPEATABLE'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('parents', 'ARRAY', 'REPEATABLE'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('teamDriveId', 'STRING'),
    bigquery.SchemaField('permissions', 'STRING')
]

# Define the table reference
table_ref = client.dataset('my_dataset').table('my_table')

# Define the table object with schema
table = bigquery.Table(table_ref, schema=schema)

# Create the table
table = client.create_table(table)

print("Table {} created.".format(table.table_id))

item.title: Google Bigquery Limit Array Elements In Bigquery Table Get First N
item.description:
How to get the first N elements from an array column in a BigQuery table without unnesting, ranking, and aggregating back to an array?

Solution A general solution with a User-Defined Function (UDF) that can be called for any array type is as follows:

CREATE TEMP FUNCTION TopN(arr ANY TYPE, n INT64) AS (
  ARRAY(SELECT x FROM UNNEST(arr) AS x WITH OFFSET off WHERE off < n ORDER BY off)
);

WITH data AS
(
  SELECT 1001 as id, ['a', 'b', 'c'] as array_1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 1002 as id, ['d', 'e', 'f', 'g'] as array_1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 1003 as id, ['h', 'i'] as array_1
)
SELECT *, TopN(array_1, 2) AS my_result
FROM data

The above code first defines a UDF called TopN that takes two inputs - an array and a number, and returns the first N elements of the array while keeping the array data type. The UDF uses UNNEST to convert the input array into a table and adds an offset to each element. It then selects the elements that have an offset less than N and orders them by offset to preserve their original order in the array. Lastly, the UDF returns an array that consists of the selected elements.

item.title: Google Bigquery Mastering Big Querys Distinct On Group By Functions
item.description:
Selecting the First Row in Each Group Using BigQuery

Summary

The aim is to select the first comment, in terms of created_utc, for each link_id (Reddit submission). It can be achieved by using GROUP BY along with ROW_NUMBER() and PARTITION BY clauses.

Dataset

The dataset used in this example is fh-bigquery:reddit_comments.2018_01.

Code Explanation

To retrieve the first comment related to each link_id, we can use the following query:

SELECT 
  ARRAY_AGG(body ORDER BY created_utc LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)] body, 
  link_id
FROM `fh-bigquery.reddit_comments.2018_01`
WHERE subreddit_id = 't5_2zkvo'
GROUP BY link_id

Here, we are using ARRAY_AGG() function that returns an array of values of a specified expression. We use body and link_id as expressions here. The LIMIT 1 argument fetches only the first row for each link_id based on its created_utc value. The OFFSET(0) argument extracts the element from the array. Lastly, we use the GROUP BY statement to group the results by link_id.

For example, let’s consider the following query:

SELECT NTH(2,SPLIT('FIRST-SECOND','-')) as second_part FROM [FOO.bar] limit 10

This query uses the SPLIT() function to split the string “FIRST-SECOND” by the “-” delimiter and selects the second substring with the NTH() function. The resulting output is “SECOND”.

select key, first(grouped_value) concat_value 
from (
    select 
        key, 
        group_concat(value, ':') over 
            (partition by key
             order by value asc
             rows between unbounded preceding and unbounded following) grouped_value
    from table_name
) 
group by key

item.title: Google Bigquery Preserving Integer Data Type In Json Export A Guide
item.description:
How to Preserve Integer Data Type when Exporting BigQuery Tables to JSON
When exporting BigQuery tables in JSON format, the INTEGER fields are converted to strings. This can be problematic for data analysis purposes since the data type is important for certain operations. This post aims to explain why this happens and provide alternative solutions to preserve integer data types.

Why are INTEGER fields converted to strings in JSON format?

The reason for this phenomenon is due to a combination of the Javascript specification, IEEE floating point precision, JSON, and BigQuery integer sizes. In Javascript, all numbers must be representable as IEEE754 double-precision floating point values. When parsing JSON numbers, Javascript numbers are used, which cannot always represent all 64-bit integer values used in BigQuery tables (which uses 64-bit signed integer values).

item.title: Google Bigquery Prevent Duplicates In Bigquery
item.description:

At times, you may encounter a situation where you would want to avoid inserting duplicates into a Bigquery table. Unfortunately, there is no primary key or unique constraint support on Bigquery. Although, there are still several ways to avoid duplicates.

The Append-only Model of Bigquery

In Bigquery, everything is append-only. That means that for any new update, a new row is added. This design choice allows us to leverage insights from every new update we add to the same row. For example, we might want to track how long it takes for the end-user to choose their country during signup flow. Since we have a dropdown of countries, it will take some time until it scrolls to their country. By appending rows for each snapshot, we can calculate the time it takes to make the selection. Moreover, we can identify how we can optimize this process using data.

item.description:
Querying BYTES Field in BigQuery Using SQL

Summary:

This Q&A Session explains how to query a BYTES field in Google BigQuery using SQL. It also provides solutions to some common errors while querying the BYTES field in BigQuery.

Querying BYTES Field in BigQuery:

BYTES is a binary data type used to store data in a byte array format. In Google BigQuery, we can use SQL to query tables that include BYTES field. To query a BYTES field, we need to use the FROM_BASE64() function to convert the Base64-encoded string to BYTES format. Here’s an example query: sql SELECT * FROM `project\_name.dataset\_name.table\_name` WHERE field_name = FROM_BASE64('16D6M7PN3w7Cn8mJyrmrUSZY9ummMf5QCGEMuiSmSlw='); In the query above, ‘16D6M7PN3w7Cn8mJyrmrUSZY9ummMf5QCGEMuiSmSlw=’ is the Base64 encoded string that we want to match with the BYTES field. More, we can also use a bytes literal that starts with ‘b’ to match the BYTES field. Here’s an updated query: sql SELECT * FROM `project\_name.dataset\_name.table\_name` WHERE field_name = b'16D6M7PN3w7Cn8mJyrmrUSZY9ummMf5QCGEMuiSmSlw='; In the query above, we are using the bytes literal ‘b’ followed by the Base64 encoded string to match the BYTES field.

item.title: Google Bigquery Querying Bigquery Table With Write_Truncate Is It Safe
item.description:
Can I safely query a BigQuery table being replaced with WRITE_TRUNCATE?

Introduction:

When a BigQuery load job is performed and the writeDisposition parameter is set to WRITE_TRUNCATE, it replaces the contents of the target table with the loaded data. During this process, users may wonder if they can query the table safely without any errors.

Answer:

Yes, it is safe to query a BigQuery table being replaced with WRITE_TRUNCATE during a load job. The WRITE_TRUNCATE is an atomic operation that gets applied at the end of the load job. Therefore, any queries that happen during that time will see either only the old data or all of the new data. There should be no cases where an error occurs while querying the table.

item.title: Google Bigquery Querying Dates In Bigquery 3 Days Prior Earlier
item.description:
Querying BigQuery Where Date is Less Than or Equal to 3 Days Minus Current Date In this post, we will discuss how to create a query in BigQuery to only return data where the date is minus 3 days from the current date. We will walk through each line of the code and provide explanations.

Query Syntax:

#standardSQL
WITH yourTable AS (
  SELECT i, date
  FROM UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY('2017-04-15', '2017-04-28')) AS date WITH OFFSET AS i
)
SELECT *
FROM yourTable
WHERE date <= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 3 DAY)

Explanation:

The query uses Standard SQL syntax in BigQuery. We start with a “WITH” clause that defines a common table expression (CTE) named “yourTable.” This CTE generates an array of dates between ‘2017-04-15’ and ‘2017-04-28’ using the GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY function. The dates are then assigned an index value using the OFFSET function.

item.title: Google Bigquery Round Timestamp To Nearest 15 Minute Intervals In Bigquery
item.description:
Question: How can I round a timestamp to the nearest 15-minute interval using BigQuery standard SQL?

Solution:

To round a timestamp to the nearest 15-minute interval in BigQuery standard SQL, you can use the following formula:

TIMESTAMP_SECONDS(900 * DIV(UNIX_SECONDS(dt_from) + 450, 900))

This formula works by converting the timestamp to Unix time (the number of seconds since January 1, 1970), adding 450 seconds (7.5 minutes) to it, dividing the result by 900 (the number of seconds in 15 minutes), rounding down to the nearest integer, and then multiplying by 900 to get the Unix time of the nearest 15-minute interval. Lastly, the Unix time is converted back to a timestamp using the TIMESTAMP_SECONDS function.

item.title: Google Bigquery Selecting Table_Id In Bigquery Table Wildcard Query
item.description:
Bigquery Table Wildcard Query using _TABLE_SUFFIX Pseudocolumn
Table Wildcard Query is used in BigQuery to query data from multiple tables with similar schema using wildcard characters. BigQuery provides the _TABLE_SUFFIX pseudocolumn that allows users to dynamically reference the table_id.

Code Explanation

The following code demonstrates the use of _TABLE_SUFFIX pseudocolumn to select all available data and group it by the column of interest and the day it was captured.

SELECT _TABLE_SUFFIX as table_id, 
       identifier, 
       Sum(AppAnalytic) as AppAnalyticCount 
FROM `database_main.Title_*` 
WHERE length(_TABLE_SUFFIX) >= 4 
GROUP BY identifier, table_id 
ORDER BY AppAnalyticCount DESC 
LIMIT 10
  • The first line of the code uses the SELECT clause to select _TABLE_SUFFIX pseudocolumn and aliases it as table_id.
  • The second line of the code selects the identifier column.
  • The third line of the code computes the sum of the AppAnalytic column and aliases it as AppAnalyticCount.
  • The fourth line of code uses the FROM clause to specify the dataset and the tables to query using wildcards. In this example, all tables with the prefix Title_ is queried.
  • The WHERE statement filters the tables that have a length greater than or equal to 4.
  • The GROUP BY clause groups the data by the identifier, and table_id columns, allowing us to analyze the data based on the day or time period.
  • The ORDER BY clause orders the data based on� AppAnalyticCount column in descending order.
  • The LIMIT clause limits the number of results returned to the top 10.

Practical Example

An example use case of this query is analyzing website traffic by capturing data on a day-sharded basis. BigQuery tables are created in a daily basis, and the rows contain time-stamped and non-time-stamped data. We can use table wildcard to retrieve data from specific tables and analyze each table to determine the web page that generated the most amount of traffic on a particular day based on their identifier.

How can I set a default value for a nullable column in BigQuery?

A nullable column can have a NULL default value, which is a trivial solution. Although, if you need to have a specific default value, you can use the field’s description to store metadata about the field, including the default value. Your application can retrieve this value from the description and use it based on its logic.

item.title: Google Bigquery Slow Apache Beam Bigqueryio Write Time

Problem The Apache Beam pipeline is writing to an unpartitioned BigQuery target table with millions of TableRows in the PCollection. BigQueryIO is creating a temp file for every single record in the BigQueryWriteTemp temp folder, leading to poor performance when running with DirectRunner. Is this behavior expected?

Solution

Yes, the behavior is expected. BigQueryIO writes TableRow objects in parallel by using a temporary file per output partition. Since the target table is unpartitioned, each TableRow will be written to its own temporary file. This can lead to an overwhelming number of temp files and poor performance when running with a DirectRunner.

item.title: Google Bigquery Stripping Non Numeric Characters From Bigquery Results
item.description:
How to Convert Dollar Amounts to Numbers in BigQuery

Problem

You have dollar amounts in your BigQuery results that you want to convert into pure numbers, but you don’t know how to do it using BigQuery functions.

Solution

You can use regular expressions to remove non-numeric characters from the dollar amounts and then cast the resulting string to an integer. Here’s an example query:

#standardSQL
WITH `project.dataset.table` AS (
  SELECT '$15,000' AS dollar_amount UNION ALL
  SELECT '$25,000' UNION ALL
  SELECT '$10,000' 
)
SELECT 
  dollar_amount, 
  CAST(REGEXP_REPLACE(dollar_amount, r'$|,', '') as INT64) amount
FROM `project.dataset.table`

The query selects the dollar amounts from the sample table project.dataset.table. It then uses the REGEXP_REPLACE function to remove the $ and , characters from each dollar amount using a regular expression. Lastly, it casts the resulting string to an INT64 using the CAST function.

When working with decimal values in Bigquery, sometimes you may find that the decimal places in your output are too long. For example, if you have a value of 0.0904246741698848, you may want to trim it down to 0.09. This can easily be done in Bigquery using the ROUND function.

item.title: Google Bigquery Understanding How Bigquerys First_Value Ignore_Nulls Work
item.description:
Learning BigQuery FIRST_VALUE and IGNORE_NULLS
In BigQuery, FIRST_VALUE is an analytic function that can be used to return the first value in a list, while IGNORE_NULLS is an optional parameter that can be included to ignore any null values in the list.

Let’s consider the following example:

WITH finishers AS (SELECT 'Bob' as name, TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 2:51:45' as finish_time, 'F30-34' as division UNION ALL SELECT NULL, TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 2:54:11', 'F35-39' UNION ALL SELECT 'Mary', TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 2:59:01', 'F35-39' UNION ALL SELECT 'John', TIMESTAMP '2016-10-18 3:01:17', 'F35-39'
)
SELECT *, FIRST_VALUE(name IGNORE NULLS) OVER(PARTITION BY division ORDER BY finish_time) AS fastest_in_division
FROM finishers
ORDER by division

This query selects data from a CTE called finishers, which contains details of a running race, including the name of each participant, the time they finished the race, and the division they competed in. The query then uses the FIRST_VALUE and IGNORE_NULLS functions to return the fastest participant in each division.

item.title: Google Bigquery Unexpected Entity Type
item.description:
Entity was of unexpected kind error when loading Firestore exports to BigQuery

Problem

When loading Firestore exports to BigQuery, you may encounter an error that says “Entity was of unexpected kind”.

Solution

  • Ensure that documents in the export data share a consistent schema. This means that each document in the collection should have the same fields with the same data types.
  • Make sure that you specify a collection-ids filter in your export command. Data exported without specifying a collection ID filter cannot be loaded into BigQuery.
  • Load data from Firestore, not from Datastore. Follow the steps given in this link to load your Firestore data to BigQuery.

Explanation

Firestore is a NoSQL document database, which means that each document in a collection can have a different structure. Although, when loading the data into BigQuery, each row in the table must have the same schema. If documents in your Firestore export data have different structures, you will encounter the “Entity was of unexpected kind” error. Another possible reason for this error is that you did not specify a collection-ids filter when exporting the data from Firestore. When exporting data, you can specify a collection-ids filter to only export data from specific collections. If you did not specify a filter and exported all data, BigQuery will not be able to determine which collection a row belongs to, resulting in the “Entity was of unexpected kind” error. Lastly, make sure that you follow the correct steps to load Firestore data to BigQuery. Loading Datastore exports to BigQuery is a different process and may not work with Firestore data.

item.title: Google Bigquery Unnesting Structs In Bigquery
item.description:
Flattening Structs with Multiple Arrays in BigQuery

Summary:

In BigQuery, if you have a struct with multiple arrays that you want to flatten to perform analysis, you can use the UNNEST operator to do so. The UNNEST operator works by converting the array into a table where each row represents an element in the original array.

Code Explanation:

sql SELECT origin, s.destination, s.visitors FROM dataset.table t CROSS JOIN UNNEST(t.struct) AS s; The code above selects data from a table called table in the dataset dataset. It then uses the CROSS JOIN command on the UNNEST operator to convert the struct column in the table into a table of elements. The UNNEST function is used twice since there are two arrays we want to flatten, destination and visitors. The AS s creates a named alias for the flattened table. s represents the flattened struct element. The columns of the flattened table can now be accessed using the alias. We can query the newly flattened table by specifying the columns we want to keep (in this case, origin, destination, and visitors). This query essentially generates a Cartesian product, where each destination is paired with every row in the visitors array.

item.title: Google Bigquery Use Cosine Similarity In Bigquery Sql
item.description:
Computing Cosine Similarity with BigQuery SQL If you have vectors stored in BigQuery and want to find the most similar between them, you can use BigQuery standard SQL to compute the cosine similarity. The following query looks at the vector defined for each document, given its dimensions (by word) and multiplies them with the cosine distance formula:

SELECT ANY_VALUE(title2) orig, ANY_VALUE(tf2id) id_orig, a.id id_similar 
  , ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE( SUM(b.tf_idf * IFNULL(c.tf_idf,0)),(SQRT(SUM(b.tf_idf*b.tf_idf))*SQRT(SUM(POW(IFNULL(c.tf_idf,0),2))))),4) distance
  , ANY_VALUE(title1) similar
  , ARRAY_AGG((ROUND(b.tf_idf,4), ROUND(c.tf_idf,4))) weights
  , ARRAY_AGG((b.word, c.word)) words
FROM (
  SELECT id, tfidfs tf1, tf2, tf2id
  , a.title title1
  , b.title title2
  FROM `your_table_name` a
  CROSS JOIN (
    SELECT tfidfs tf2, id tf2id, title 
    FROM `your_table_name`
    WHERE id = 11353679 
    LIMIT 1
  ) b
) a
, UNNEST(tf1) b LEFT JOIN UNNEST(tf2) c ON b.word=c.word
GROUP BY id
ORDER BY distance DESC

CREATE TEMP FUNCTION RADIANS(x FLOAT64) AS (
  ACOS(-1) * x / 180
);
CREATE TEMP FUNCTION RADIANS_TO_KM(x FLOAT64) AS (
  111.045 * 180 * x / ACOS(-1)
);
CREATE TEMP FUNCTION HAVERSINE(lat1 FLOAT64, long1 FLOAT64,
                               lat2 FLOAT64, long2 FLOAT64) AS (
  RADIANS_TO_KM(
    ACOS(COS(RADIANS(lat1)) * COS(RADIANS(lat2)) *
         COS(RADIANS(long1) - RADIANS(long2)) +
         SIN(RADIANS(lat1)) * SIN(RADIANS(lat2))))
);

item.title: Google Bigquery Using Select Into In Bigquery
item.description:
How to use SELECT INTO with BigQuery

Summary

In MySQL, Oracle and Teradata, the SELECT ... INTO FROM ... statement is used to retrieve values from a table and assign them to variables. BigQuery, on the other hand, uses a SET statement to assign values from a subquery to variables.

Syntax

The syntax for the SET statement in BigQuery is as follows:

SET (variable1, variable2, variable3) = (SELECT AS STRUCT column1, column2, column3 FROM table_name WHERE condition LIMIT 1)

Here, we assign the values of column1, column2, and column3 to variable1, variable2, and variable3, respectively, from a table called table_name where a certain condition is met. The LIMIT 1 clause ensures that only one row is returned.

item.title: Google Bigquery Using Sql Udf In Join Predicate With Bigquery
item.description:
Querying BigQuery with SQL UDF in join predicate
When querying BigQuery and using a SQL User-Defined Function (UDF) in a join predicate, an error might occur with the message “Subquery in join predicate should only depend on exactly one join side.” This error is caused by a limitation of query planning and optimization.

Example:

The following code demonstrates an example of using a SQL UDF in a join predicate:

CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION game_match(game1 STRING, game2 STRING) AS (
  strpos(game1,game2) >0
);

SELECT 
  t1.gameId 
FROM `bigquery-public-data.baseball.games_post_wide` t1
LEFT JOIN `bigquery-public-data.baseball.games_post_wide` t2 
  ON t1.gameId=t2.gameId AND game_match(t1.gameId, t2.gameId)

The game_match function returns true if the second string is found within the first string and false otherwise. The query selects the gameId from the left table while joining the table on the gameId field and using the game_match function in the join predicate.

item.title: Handling Division by Zero Error in BigQuery

When working with calculations in BigQuery that involve division, there is a risk of encountering “division by zero” errors. To mitigate this issue, you can use the SAFE_DIVIDE function or the NULLIF function. Let’s explore both methods:

Using SAFE_DIVIDE Function

The SAFE_DIVIDE function provides a safe way to perform division and returns NULL when the divisor is zero. Here’s an example:

ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(CASE WHEN Name LIKE '%MIKE%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), COUNT(Name) * 100), 1) AS Percentage_of_MIKE

Explanation:

  • The SUM function counts the occurrences of ‘MIKE’ in the Name column.
  • The COUNT function calculates the total number of names.
  • The SAFE_DIVIDE function safely divides the count of ‘MIKE’ by the total count of names, multiplying the result by 100.
  • The ROUND function rounds off the result to one decimal place.
