item.title: Hibernate Oracle Sequence Gap
item.description:
Hibernate Oracle Sequence Gap Explanation of Hibernate Oracle Sequence Producing Large Gap

Summary

In this code, an Oracle sequence is used for generating subject IDs when creating new subjects. The Hibernate framework is used for handling database operations. Although, the sequence produces a large gap in the subject IDs.

Explanation

The table ‘subject’ is created with the following columns: SUBJECT_ID, FNAME, LNAME, EMAILADR, and BIRTHDT. The SUBJECT_ID column is defined as the primary key of the table using the data_index tablespace. A sequence named ‘sub_seq’ is created with a minimum value of 1, maximum value of 999999999999999999999999999, cached in blocks of 100 with no cycle. This sequence is used for generating new subject IDs. The Subject class is defined as an entity using the @Entity and @Table annotations. The @Id annotation specifies that the subjectId field is mapped to the SUBJECT_ID column in the ‘subject’ table. The @GeneratedValue annotation specifies that the subjectId field is generated using a sequence named ‘SUB_SEQ’. The @SequenceGenerator annotation provides additional configuration for the ‘SUB_SEQ’ sequence. When a new subject is added using Hibernate, the sequence number jumps to 255050 resulting in large gaps in the subject IDs. This is because the sequence is cached and values are pulled from the cache in blocks of 100 to improve performance. The cache size can be adjusted to reduce the size of the gaps.

item.description:
How to Delete Oracle Schema Contents Quickly or any other Q&A website without proper attribution and confirmation from the author/owner.

How can I delete all contents in a schema in Oracle?
To delete all contents in a schema in Oracle, you can use the following script:

BEGIN
   FOR cur_rec IN (SELECT object_name, object_type
                   FROM user_objects
                   WHERE object_type IN ('TABLE', 'VIEW', 'PACKAGE', 'SEQUENCE', 'MATERIALIZED VIEW'))
   LOOP
      BEGIN
         EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('DROP ' || cur_rec.object_type || ' "' || cur_rec.object_name || '" CASCADE CONSTRAINTS');
      EXCEPTION
         WHEN OTHERS THEN
            DBMS_OUTPUT.put_line ('FAILED: DROP ' || cur_rec.object_type || ' "' || cur_rec.object_name || '": ' || SQLERRM);
      END;
   END LOOP;
END;
/

This script will drop all tables, views, packages, sequences, and materialized views in the schema. It also drops their associated constraints.

item.title: How To Get List Of Tables In Google Bigquery Ordered By Size
item.description:
Get List of Google BigQuery Tables Order By Size
When working with Google BigQuery to store and analyze data, foremost to keep track of the size of your tables to optimize performance and minimize storage costs. Luckily, BigQuery offers a simple way to get a list of tables ordered by size using Standard SQL.

The Code:

#standardSQL
SELECT table_id,
    DATE(TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(creation_time)) AS creation_date,
    DATE(TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(last_modified_time)) AS last_modified_date,
    row_count,
    size_bytes,
    CASE
        WHEN type = 1 THEN 'table'
        WHEN type = 2 THEN 'view'
        WHEN type = 3 THEN 'external'
        ELSE '?'
    END AS type,
    TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(creation_time) AS creation_time,
    TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(last_modified_time) AS last_modified_time,
    dataset_id,
    project_id
FROM `yourProject.yourDataset.__TABLES__`
ORDER BY size_bytes DESC

Explanation:

  • The first line specifies the use of Standard SQL by using the #standardSQL directive.
  • The SELECT statement selects the columns or expressions to be retrieved from the tables.
  • table_id identifies the name of the table.
  • creation_date and last_modified_date represent the date when the table was created and last modified respectively, in the format of yyyy-mm-dd.
  • row_count represents the total number of rows in the table.
  • size_bytes represents the total size of the table in bytes.
  • CASE statement maps the integer values of type column to their corresponding string values representing the type of the table, namely: table, view, external; or a question mark if the value is unknown.
  • creation_time and last_modified_time represent the date and time when the table was created and last modified respectively, in UNIX timestamp format.
  • dataset_id and project_id represent the ID of the dataset and project where the table resides.
  • The FROM statement specifies the source tables or views from which to retrieve data. In this case, __TABLES__ represents a system table that lists all tables in the specified dataset.
  • The ORDER BY clause sorts the resulting rows by the specified column or expression, in descending order.

Practical Example:

You can run the above query directly in the BigQuery web UI or API to get a list of tables in a specific dataset ordered by size. This can help you identify tables that are occupying more space and decide whether to optimize them or archive them to reduce storage costs.

long_raw_length_function(long_col) + DBMS_LOB.GETLENGTH(blob_col) 
FROM table 
WHERE id_col = id_val;

The vsize function returns the size in bytes of a column, while the long_raw_length_function function returns the length of a LONG RAW column. The DBMS_LOB.GETLENGTH function returns the length of a BLOB column. By adding the sizes of all columns, you can obtain the actual size of a row in bytes.

item.title: How To Prevent Sql Injection In Oracles Order By Clause
item.description:
Preventing SQL Injection in Oracle “ORDER BY” Query with NamedParameterJdbcTemplate

When creating an SQL query with a sorting “ORDER BY” part, it’s crucial to prevent SQL Injection attacks. This is done by using parameter maps to prevent injection in the “where” part of the query. Although, since there’s no automatic escaping for the “ORDER BY” part, it’s more prone to SQL Injection attacks. item.title: How To Remove Duplicate Rows Based On Attribute In Google Bigquery Sql
item.description:
Removing Duplicate Rows According to an Attribute in Google BigQuery SQL
In order to remove duplicate rows in a Google BigQuery table, we can use the ROW_NUMBER() analytic function in combination with a subquery. Here’s an example:

SELECT
  *
FROM (
  SELECT
    *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY transactionid ORDER BY transactionid) rownum
  FROM
    result
)
WHERE
  rownum = 1

First, the inner query selects all columns and rows from the result table, and adds a new column called rownum using ROW_NUMBER(). The PARTITION BY clause tells BigQuery to partition the data by the transactionid column, and the ORDER BY clause sorts the partitions by the same column. This means that for each unique transactionid, rows will be numbered starting from 1.

item.description:
Insert Data on Oracle Only if Row is Absent How to insert a row in Oracle only if it does not already exist?

One option is to use a MERGE statement that allows you to perform INSERT or UPDATE operations based on a condition.

Example

merge into table1 t1
using (select 'value1' as value1, value2 
       from table2 
       where table2.type="ok") t2
on (t1.col1 = t2.value1)
when not matched then
  insert (t1.col1, t1.col2) 
  values (t2.value1, t2.value2);

In this example, the MERGE statement joins the rows from table1 and table2 based on the equality of their columns (col1 and value1). If a matching row exists in table1, the MERGE statement updates its values with those of the corresponding row in table2, otherwise, it inserts the values from the row in table2 into the table1.

item.title: Invalid Cast Error Oracleconnection Not Recognized As Connection Type
item.description:
Invalid Cast Error: OracleConnection Not Recognized as Connection Type How to cast Connection to OracleConnection in Java?
If you are trying to cast Connection to OracleConnection and receiving a ClassCastException, it is probably because the connection retrieved is a Wrapped Connection. You need to retrieve the underlying connection and then cast it to OracleConnection.

Step-by-step explanation of the code:

Let us go through the code line by line:

@Repository
public class AuditLogDAOImpl implements AuditLogDAO {

    @PersistenceContext(unitName="myUnitName")
    EntityManager em;

    @Resource(name = "dataSource")
    DataSource dataSource;

    public void init() {

        try {
            Connection connection = DataSourceUtils.getConnection(dataSource);
            connection = ((org.jboss.resource.adapter.jdbc.WrappedConnection)connection).getUnderlyingConnection(); //Get the underlying connection from wrapped connection
            OracleConnection oracleConnection = (OracleConnection) connection; //Cast connection to OracleConnection

            String metrics[] = new String[OracleConnection.END_TO_END_STATE_INDEX_MAX];
            metrics[OracleConnection.END_TO_END_CLIENTID_INDEX] = "my_new_username";

            oracleConnection.setEndToEndMetrics(metrics, (short) 0);

            java.util.Properties props = new java.util.Properties();
            props.put("osuser", "newValue");

            oracleConnection.setClientInfo(props);

        } catch (SQLException e) {
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
    }
}

The code retrieves a Connection from the dataSource and then retrieves the underlying connection from a Wrapped Connection. The underlying connection is then cast to OracleConnection.

What is the Default Sort Order?

The default sort order in MongoDB is an undefined implementation detail. This means that MongoDB does not guarantee any particular order when it comes to sorting records. However, for capped collections, MongoDB does guarantee that the results will be returned in the insertion order.

Are you feeling stuck while finding an equivalent of DECODE() function in MySQL? Well, you are just in the right place. This post will guide you to resolve your confusion.

Learning the Problem

The DECODE() function is a handy function in Oracle that returns a value by comparing a given expression with a list of values. If the expression matches any value from the list, then the corresponding result is returned. It takes a minimum of three arguments: the expression to evaluate, the search value, and the result value. Optional pairs of search value and result value can follow. If the expression does not match any value from the list, then the default result value is returned. Although, MySQL does not provide a DECODE() function out of the box. But you can achieve the same functionality with different options.

Azure Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model database service that enables you to manage large amounts of data across a variety of platforms and data models. Given its extensive feature set, you may have some queries about Azure Cosmos DB’s multi-model nature.

What does it mean that Azure Cosmos DB is multi-model?

Azure Cosmos DB is a single NoSQL data engine that can support multiple data models including documents, key-value, graph, and column-family. The database engine is based on the atom-record-sequence (ARS), which consists of atoms, records, and sequences. The different data models are projected and translated onto the ARS-based data model, and the core data model of Cosmos DB is natively accessible from dynamically-typed programming languages and can be exposed as JSON.

item.description:
NOSQL: C in CAP is different from C in ACID: Here’s why Why is C in CAP theorem not the same as C in ACID?

Summary:

The C in CAP theorem and the C in ACID both stand for consistency but have different meanings. In CAP, consistency means that all nodes see the same data at the same time, while in ACID, it means that any transaction the database performs will take it from one consistent state to another.

What is Cassandra Data Model?
Cassandra is a NoSQL database that uses a hybrid data model comprising elements of both a row-oriented and a column-oriented database. Cassandra still organizes data into rows and columns, like a traditional relational database, but with a few significant differences.

Introduction

Cassandra is a popular NoSQL database known for its ability to handle high write volume and high availability. Although, achieving maximum write performance with Cassandra can be challenging. In this blog post, we will discuss how to improve write performance in Cassandra.

Learning Write Performance in Cassandra

Before we dive into improving write performance, it’s important to know how Cassandra stores data. Cassandra stores data in a data structure called a “partition.” Each partition corresponds to a row in a table and is identified by a partition key. Within a partition, data is further organized into columns. Each partition is assigned to a node in the Cassandra cluster based on its partition key.

item.description:
NoSQL Databases: Indexes - Use or Need? Do NoSQL databases use or need indexes?
NoSQL databases are gaining popularity because of their scalability, flexibility, and high-performance capabilities. Although, one question that often comes up is whether NoSQL databases use or need indexes. In general, the answer is yes.

Why do NoSQL databases need indexes?

Although NoSQL databases use various data models, such as key-value, document, column family, and graph, they all share a common need for efficient data retrieval. To achieve that, NoSQL databases use indexes to quickly locate data within their datasets. Indexes can enhance the database’s performance by reducing the time needed to perform queries and fetch records.

This means that data is duplicated and stored in multiple documents, to eliminate the need for joins, which are not possible in NoSQL databases. item.description:

Summary:

MongoDB and Cassandra are both amazing NoSQL databases, but they differ in their read and write performance. Cassandra is known for its excellent write performance, whereas MongoDB is known for its superior read performance. In this post, we will explore the myths and realities surrounding MongoDB vs. Cassandra’s read/write performance.

Write Performance:

Cassandra’s write performance is better than MongoDB’s when dealing with large datasets. This is because Cassandra’s storage engine provides constant-time writes, no matter how big the data set is. On the other hand, MongoDB’s write performance suffers due to two reasons: the b-tree based storage engine and the per-database write lock. Although, foremost to note that MongoDB supports a lock per document, not per database, as previously claimed.

If you are working with a schemaless document database like MongoDB, you might wonder how inheritance can be handled. In traditional relational databases, inheritance is implemented using concepts like “table-per-hierarchy” or “table-per-class”.

Although, in MongoDB collections contain documents with different structures, so inheritance can be handled differently. Let’s see how.

Assume we have two classes: A and B, where B inherits from A. In a traditional RDBMS, we would create two tables: A with columns X, Y, and Z, and B with columns X,Y,Z, and W. But in MongoDB, we don’t need to create separate collections for A and B, we can store documents of both types in the same collection.

item.title: Nosql Enforcing Foreign Keys In Mongodb A Guide
item.description:
NOSQL: Enforcing Foreign Keys in MongoDB: A Guide In this blog post, we will discuss how to enforce foreign keys in NoSQL databases, specifically MongoDB. We will take an example of a collection of documents and how to reference them to another collection.

Let’s say we have a collection of documents as follows:

{ "_id" : 0 , "owner":0 "name":"Doc1"},{ "_id" : 1 , "owner":1, "name":"Doc1"}, etc

				  On the other hand, we have a collection of owners:  
				  

{ "_id" : 0 , "username":"John"}, { "_id" : 1 , "username":"Sam"}

Now we want to ensure that when we insert a document, it references the user in a correct way. In old-school RDBMS, this can easily be done using a foreign key, but MongoDB doesn’t have foreign keys. To handle this, we can check the correctness of the insertion from the business code, but what if an attacker tampers with the request to the server and puts “owner”: 100, and MongoDB doesn’t throw any exception back? To address this situation, we need to ensure that only the application can insert data that follows our referential integrity rules. MongoDB encourages handling foreign-key relationships on the client-side. Still, they also provide the idea of “Database References” - See this help page. Although, using a DBRef is not recommended. Instead, we can embed the owner’s “documents” inside the owner object itself. This is a one-to-one relationship, and it is better to maintain them as embeddings rather than separate collections. Embedding gives us the same effect as foreign key constraints. To embed one document in another, we can model them in MongoDB as follows:

item.title: Nosql Exploring Hamming Distance Similarity Searches In Databases
item.description: NOSQL: Exploring Hamming Distance and Similarity Searches in Databases Summary: The problem at hand is retrieving records from a database based on the similarity of their 32-bit perceptual hashes. The solution presented involves dividing the hash bit string into smaller chunks and querying for an exact match on these chunks. The returned results are then subjected to a bitwise hamming distance computation to determine the actual similarity between the queried hash and the records in the database. This approach is based on a technique called simhash, and was first described by Moses Charikar in a paper.

item.title: Nosql Optimizing Social Network Schema Design
item.description: NOSQL: Optimizing Social Network Schema Design or any other online forum as a primary source. As a developer working on a proof of concept app for a social network, you may be wondering about how best to design the ‘schema’ for your app. One of the primary concerns may be whether to embed a user’s subscriptions or have a separate ‘subscriptions’ collection and use db references. Let’s explore this in detail. ### Embedding subscriptions vs having a separate collection If you choose to embed a user’s subscriptions, you will need to perform a query to get all of a user’s followers. For example, given the following user: { "username" : "alan", "photo": "123.jpg", "subscriptions" : [ {"username" : "john", "status" : "accepted"}, {"username" : "paul", "status" : "pending"} ] } To find all of alan’s subscribers, you’d have to run something like this: db.users.find({'subscriptions.username' : 'alan'}); Although, MongoDB can place indexes on elements which are arrays, so that will make things a lot faster if you are looking for how many friendships a user has. On the other hand, having a separate ‘subscriptions’ collection and using db references can also be a good way to design your schema. This can help reduce the amount of data stored in a single document, making it easier to manage and scale. It can also help to avoid duplicate data, which can become a problem when storing large amounts of data. Although, it may require more complex queries to fetch data in certain cases. ### Recommendations for displaying a list of subscriptions/subscribers When displaying a list of subscriptions/subscribers, you may encounter problems with n+1 because the subscription document only tells you the username of the target user but not other attributes like the profile photo. One way to solve this issue is to use the $lookup pipeline stage in MongoDB. This stage allows you to perform a join-like operation between documents in different collections, based on a common field. For example, to fetch the profile photos of a user’s subscribers, you can run a query like this: db.users.aggregate([ { $match: { username: 'alan' } }, { $lookup: { from: 'users', localField: 'subscriptions.username', foreignField: 'username', as: 'subscribers' } }, { $unwind: '$subscribers', }, { $project: { 'subscribers.username': 1, 'subscribers.photo': 1 } } ]); This query fetches the user document for ‘alan’, and then performs a lookup against the ‘users’ collection, using the ‘subscriptions.username’ field as the local field, and the ‘username’ field as the foreign field. It then adds the fetched documents to a new field called ‘subscribers’. After that, it unwinds the ‘subscribers’ array so that each subscriber becomes a separate document. Lastly, it uses the $project stage to only include the ‘username’ and ‘photo’ fields of the subscriber documents. ### Recap When designing the ‘schema’ for a social network app, the decision to embed subscriptions or have a separate collection with db references depends largely on the specific requirements and use cases of the app. Both approaches have their pros and cons, and careful consideration should be given to each before making a final decision. When displaying a list of subscriptions/subscribers, the $lookup pipeline stage in MongoDB can be a amazing tool to include additional information from related documents.]]>

item.title: Nosql Pros Cons Of Migrating From Mysql To Cassandra
item.description:
NOSQL: Pros and Cons of Migrating from MySQL to Cassandra

Switching from MySQL to Cassandra - Pros/Cons?

If you are thinking about switching from MySQL to Cassandra, you may be wondering about the pros and cons of making such a move. In this Q&A-style post, we will explore what you need to know to make an informed decision.

What are some of the benefits of using Cassandra over MySQL?

  • Scalability: Cassandra is designed to be highly scalable, making it ideal for managing large amounts of data. It is capable of handling a huge volume of both reads and writes.
  • Automatic replication: Cassandra automatically replicates your data across multiple nodes, providing redundancy and high availability.
  • High performance: Cassandra is specifically built for performance, with its distributed architecture enabling lightning-fast data access and retrieval.
  • NoSQL data model: Cassandra’s NoSQL data model is highly flexible, allowing for dynamic and complex data structures.

What are some of the drawbacks of switching to Cassandra?

  • Learning curve: Unless you are familiar with NoSQL databases, there may be a learning curve when switching to Cassandra.
  • Query language: Cassandra uses a different query language than SQL, so queries will need to be re-written.
  • No ACID compliance: Cassandra does not support ACID compliance like MySQL, so data consistency can be more complex to manage.

What are the key features I need to consider for my data model?

  • Order by: Cassandra’s SliceRange can satisfy this requirement.
  • Group by: Since Cassandra is a NoSQL database, grouping is not a feature supported out-of-the-box as it is in SQL. Although, it is possible to implement a similar functionality through the use of map reduce.
  • Many-to-many relations: Cassandra SuperColumns can do well for one-to-many relationships.
  • Full-text search: Lucandra project provides a full-text engine similar to Sphinx in MySQL.

What size of data and workload can I expect to handle on a medium EC2 instance if I switch to Cassandra?

On a medium EC2 instance, you can expect a significant improvement in reads and writes over MySQL. Cassandra’s distributed architecture and built-in replication make it highly effective for handling large amounts of data and high traffic workloads. That being said, you should always consider your specific workload and data requirements before making the switch.

item.title: Nosql Significance Of Eventual Consistency In Cassandra
item.description:
NOSQL: The Significance of Eventual Consistency in Cassandra Learning Eventual Consistency in Cassandra

Introduction to Eventual Consistency in Cassandra

Cassandra is a popular NoSQL database system known for its scalability and fault-tolerance. One of the core concepts of Cassandra is eventual consistency, which is different from traditional SQL databases that emphasize immediate consistency. In Cassandra, data is distributed and replicated among multiple nodes in a cluster, which means that there may be different versions of the same data on different nodes at the same time. The nodes in a single cluster do not contain identical copies of the same data, instead of making it distributed, which makes immediate consistency impossible. In this Q&A Session, we will explain what eventual consistency means in Cassandra, how it works, and how it affects Cassandra’s performance.

The question is about storing a list of items in DynamoDB for a parent object. The parent object has attributes and a list of objects. The size of the list can vary. The author wants to know whether to keep each list’s item as a separate record or split the list’s items into multiple records.

Answer:

The approach depends on the Query Access Pattern (QAP). If you need to retrieve all the list items at once, it’s best to keep each item as a separate record. If you need to retrieve a subset of items or run queries on the list items, it’s best to split the list items into multiple records.

item.title: Nosql Understanding Eventual Consistency A Simple Explanation
item.description:
NOSQL: Understanding Eventual Consistency: A Simple Explanation

Learning Eventual Consistency in Plain English

Eventual consistency is a popular term used in NoSQL, data grids and other distributed storage systems. It is defined as the state of a distributed system, in which all nodes in the system eventually have the same data, after a certain amount of time, even if there are changes being made to it in the meantime.

In simpler terms, eventual consistency means that updates or changes to data in a distributed system are not instantly propagated to all nodes in the system. Instead, it can take some amount of time for updates to reach all nodes, leading to temporary inconsistencies in the data. Eventually, all nodes will have the same consistent view of the data.

Summary To average time intervals in Oracle 10g, a SQL query can be used. The average can be calculated using the formula avg(endtime-starttime). Although, there may be inconsistencies in datatypes, which can be solved by converting the duration into seconds using the extract() function. A more efficient way is to use the formula: (sysdate + (endtime - starttime)*24*60*60 - sysdate) If the endtime and starttime aren’t within a second of each other, then you can cast the timestamps as dates and use date arithmetic for the calculation.

item.title: Oracle Aggregating Boolean Columns A Step By Step Guide
item.description:
ORACLE: Aggregating Boolean Columns: A Step-by-Step Guide Aggregating a Boolean Column Explained
Aggregating a Boolean column means to apply an operation that combines multiple rows into a single value. In this case, we want to combine a set of tuples that contain Boolean values using the OR function, and return the result as a single tuple with aggregated Boolean values.

Approach

The easiest way to do this is to use the MAX() function to determine whether a particular Boolean value is present in the group. Since the Boolean data type can be represented as an integer where 1 = True and 0 = False, we can use the MAX() function to find the highest value in the group, which would correspond to the Boolean value of True. Therefore, if a True value is present in the group, then the MAX() function would return 1, which would indicate that the final aggregated value is True. Otherwise, the MAX() function would return 0, which would indicate that the final aggregated value is False.

Code Explanation The following code selects all the records from the order_header table where the tran_date column is equal to yesterday’s date.

select  *
from    order_header oh
where   tran_date = sysdate-1

The sysdate function returns the current date and time. By subtracting one from it, we get yesterday’s date. Although, this code may not always work as expected because the tran_date column may contain timestamps, making it difficult to compare with a full date. To select records only from yesterday, we need to extract the date portion of the tran_date column and compare it to yesterday’s date. One way to do this is to use the trunc function, which returns the date portion of a datetime value. We can use it to truncate both the tran_date and sysdate-1 values to their respective dates and compare them.

If you have a list of known values that you want to use in a CTE (Common Table Expression), you can include them using the UNION ALL syntax in Oracle.

Creating a CTE with Hard-Coded Values

To create a CTE with hard-coded values in Oracle, you can use the following syntax:

WITH cte AS (
  SELECT 101 id FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 102 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 105 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 200 FROM dual
)
SELECT *
FROM cte;

In this example, the WITH statement is used to create a CTE named cte that includes four hard-coded values: 101, 102, 105, and 200. The UNION ALL syntax is used to combine these four values into a single result set.

ORACLE: Database Throughput: A Quick Explanation What is Database Throughput?
When discussing the performance of a database management system, many technical terms come into play. “Throughput” is one of them. But what does it really mean?

Learning the Definition of Throughput

In network communications, throughput refers to the successful delivery of messages over a communication channel. In database management, throughput defines the number of transactions a system can handle per unit of time. In the context of an OLTP database, or an online transaction processing database, throughput is the number of transactions it can process in a second.

item.title: Oracle Date Time Addition Standards What Are They
item.description: ORACLE: Date/Time Addition Standards: What Are They? Standards for adding dates and times can differ across different programming languages and tools. One common concern is what happens when adding a month to a date - should the result be the last day of the next month, the first day of the month after that, or something else entirely? While there is no universal standard for this, some programming languages and organizations have outlined their own guidelines. For example, the POSIX.1-2001 standard suggests adjusting the values until they fit, which can result in different dates depending on the month and year. Meanwhile, SQL-92 considers asking for the next month from January 31 to be an error. Ultimately, the choice of how to handle date and time addition can depend on the specific requirements of the project or domain. It’s essential to carefully consider how different options could impact the functionality and usability of the application.

procedure_name(

);

Introduction

In Oracle, subtypes are a way to create new types from existing ones, with additional constraints. Although, this can sometimes result in a lot of redundant code, especially if you need to write the same functions and procedures for different subtypes. In this blog post, we will explore some ways to eliminate subtype dependency in Oracle.

The Problem

Let’s consider the following example. We have a package called “so1” that defines two subtypes - “foo_t” and “bar_t”. We also have two associated types - “foolist” and “barlist”, which are table types of “foo_t” and “bar_t” respectively. We then have two procedures called “set”, one for each subtype, which takes an ID and a list of values as input, and inserts them into a table called “so1table”. Lastly, we have two functions called “to_str”, again one for each subtype, which converts a list of values into a string.

item.description:

Summary:

What Causes the Error?

The most likely cause of this error is that the user attempting to add the FK constraint (LAB_ADMIN_USER) does not have the necessary permissions to reference the PK table (LAB_ADMIN.TEST_TEMPLATE). This table is owned by a different schema, and the owning user must grant REFERENCES permissions to the user adding the FK constraint.

item.title: Oracle How To Check If A Database Table Contains Data With Sql Code
item.description:
ORACLE: How to Check if a Database Table Contains Data with SQL Code In this question, the user wants to check a condition based on the count of a column from a table. If the count is greater than zero, they want to update the same table, otherwise, they do not want to update it.

The initial code provided is as follows:

if (select count(column) from table) > 0 then   if (condition) > 0 then     update table   else      do not update   end if; end if; ```  Here, if the count of the column is greater than zero, the inner if condition is evaluated. If it is greater than zero, the table is updated, and if it is not, the table is not updated. Although, this code might not work in certain databases like Oracle.  Therefore, a better way to write this code would be:  ``` declare   value\_count number; begin   select count(column) into value\_count from table;      if value\_count > 0 then     if (condition) > 0 then       update table     else       -- do not update     end if;   end if; end; ```  Here, we first declare a variable `value\_count` of `number` datatype. We then use the `select` statement to count the number of rows in the table and store the result in the `value\_count` variable using the `into` keyword.  After that, we check if the `value\_count` is greater than zero. If it is, we evaluate the inner `if` condition. If the condition is true, we update the table, otherwise, we do not update it.  It is to be noted that the code within the `else` block of the inner `if` condition is not required as it does nothing when executed. It can be removed to reduce the complexity of the code.  An alternative way to accomplish the same task would be to use a single SQL statement:  ``` update table set column = new\_value where (select count(column) from table) > 0 and (condition) > 0; ```  Here, we use the `update` statement to update the table `set`ting the value of `column` to the `new\_value`, but only if the count of rows in the table is greater than zero and the `condition` is true.  To summarize, we can use either PL/SQL or SQL statements to achieve the goal of updating a table based on a count of rows from another table. In PL/SQL, we can declare a variable, use the `select` statement to count rows, and then evaluate the conditions using `if` statements. In SQL, we can use the `update` statement with appropriate `where` clauses to accomplish the task.]]>

item.title: Oracle How To Delete All Data From Every Sql Table
item.description:
ORACLE: How to Delete All Data from Every SQL Table? How to Delete All Data from All Tables in Oracle DB

If you are maintaining more than 30 tables in Oracle DB and want to delete all the data from these tables without dropping the tables, you can use the following SQL code:

BEGIN
  FOR c IN (SELECT table_name, constraint_name FROM user_constraints WHERE constraint_type='R')
  LOOP
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('alter table ' || c.table_name || ' disable constraint ' || c.constraint_name);
  END LOOP;
  FOR c IN (SELECT table_name FROM user_tables)
  LOOP
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('truncate table ' || c.table_name);
  END LOOP;
  FOR c IN (SELECT table_name, constraint_name FROM user_constraints WHERE constraint_type='R')
  LOOP
    EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ('alter table ' || c.table_name || ' enable constraint ' || c.constraint_name);
  END LOOP;
END;

This code first disables all referential integrity constraints for all tables. It then truncates all the tables to delete all data. Lastly, it enables all the referential integrity constraints for all tables.

What is AutoCommit Behavior?

AutoCommit behavior determines whether or not every individual SQL statement is automatically committed right after it is executed. When a connection is created, it is in AutoCommit mode by default. This means that every SQL statement is treated as a transaction, and it is automatically committed right after it is executed. Although, the default behavior is for a SQL statement to be committed when it is completed, not when it is executed. A statement is considered completed when all of its result sets and update counts have been retrieved. In almost all cases, a statement is completed, and therefore committed, right after it is executed, but foremost to keep this behavior in mind when working with JDBC.

public class oraDbContext : DbContext

    internal void OnModelCreating(DbModelBuilder modelBuilder) {
        modelBuilder.Configurations.Add(new someTableMap());
    }
}

item.title: Oracle Mechanics Of Pl Sqls Contains Function Explained
item.description:
ORACLE: The Mechanics of PL-SQL’s contains() Function Explained Summary:

The PL-SQL contains() method is used on text fields that have a ‘CONTEXT Index’ to search for specific strings. It counts how many times a string occurs in a text field and returns the rows where the string exists.

The standard usage of contains() is as follows:

SELECT score(1), value FROM table_name WHERE CONTAINS(textField, ‘searchString’, 1) > 0; Explanation: The above query is used to find rows where the string ‘searchString’ exists in the textField of the table. The ‘score’ operator is used to display the results based on the number of times the string is found in the text field. For example, if we have a table named ’table_name’ with three columns - value, textField, and id - and the following data: value | textField |— 2 | A 1 | C Explanation of the code example: The code example from Oracle’s documentation is used to display the top 10 news Q&A Sessions that contain the word ‘oracle’. The code starts by declaring a variable named ‘rowno’ and initializing it to 0. It then uses a ‘for loop’ to iterate through the results of the query. The query selects the score and title from the ’news’ table where the ’text’ column contains the word ‘oracle’. The loop increases the ‘rowno’ variable by 1 for each iteration and outputs the title and score of the current row using the ‘dbms_output.put_line’ function. The code exits the loop after outputting the top 10 rows using the ’exit when rowno = 10;’ statement. Rewritten code: DECLARE rowno NUMBER := 0; BEGIN FOR c1 IN ( SELECT SCORE(1) score, title FROM news WHERE CONTAINS(text, ‘oracle’, 1) > 0 ORDER BY SCORE(1) DESC ) LOOP rowno := rowno + 1; DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(c1.title||’: ‘||c1.score); EXIT WHEN rowno = 10; END LOOP; END; Practical examples: The contains() method can be used in many practical scenarios, such as searching for specific words in text fields or finding relevant documents. For example, a company may use contains() to search for resumes that match specific keywords when hiring new employees. Another practical use case is searching for relevant documents in legal cases by using keywords. Alternative ways: If you cannot use contains(), you can use the ’like’ operator to search for specific strings in text fields. Although, like does not provide the same level of accuracy and speed as contains() since it does not use a CONTEXT Index. Another alternative is using regular expressions to search for specific patterns in text fields. Regular expressions can be amazing, but they can also be complex and may not be as efficient as contains() for large datasets. References: - Oracle: https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/ccapp/overview-text-query-language.html - DBA Oracle: http://www.dba-oracle.com/t _sql_contains_clause.htm]]>

item.description:

Solution: There are a few possible solutions to this issue:

  1. Set the Oracle client path: To use the Oracle OCI driver, the relevant .dll files need to be present in the Java library path. Ensure that the correct release (both in terms of 32/64 bit and version number) is being used. Alternatively, you can set the Oracle client path by navigating to Tools -> Preference -> Database -> Advanced -> Use Oracle client and choosing the correct path. 2. Check for missing files: Ensure that the external folder of the .ora files is still present. If not, point to it again via (menu navigation): Tools -> Preferences -> Database -> Advanced -> tnsnames directory. 3. Reconnect using connection property: Enter the connection property and from this level, reconnect. 4. Rename system folder: If you are using JDeveloper 12c and encounter this issue, rename the C:\Users\username\AppData\Roaming\JDeveloper\System folder, run the project from JDeveloper, close JDeveloper, rename back the System folder and try running the project again. 5. Set up environment variable: For JDeveloper 12c, set up an environment variable that refers to the ojdbc jar by adding the following command: -J-Djdbc.library=ojdbc6.jar".

It is recommended to check the Oracle documentation for more information and detailed instructions on resolving this issue.]]>

item.title: Oracle Optimizing Clob Performance With Substr Function
item.description:
ORACLE: Optimizing CLOB Performance with SUBSTR Function or any other forum as a reference, only use reputable sources.)

In a PL/SQL procedure, SUBSTR is used extensively on a VARCHAR2 parameter. To remove the length limit, the parameter was changed to a CLOB, but performance was observed to suffer. This prompted a series of tests to determine the cause of the decreased performance, based on previous experiments from 2005. The test results show that SUBSTR(VARCHAR2) is the fastest, followed by DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR, and then CLOB SUBSTR. This contradicts previous test results and prompts the question of why this is happening. To further investigate, the test was expanded by increasing the string length to 30 characters and performing 10 test runs. The results showed VARCHAR2 SUBSTR performed fastest, while CLOB SUBSTR had the worst performance. Although, DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR performed similarly to VARCHAR2 SUBSTR. Changing the substring range to 5,14 (14,5 for DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR), and then to 17,14 (14,17 for DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR), resulted in DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR still performing similarly to VARCHAR2 SUBSTR, while CLOB SUBSTR performance continued to lag behind. It is important to note that the specific hardware and Oracle versions used in the experiment may have an impact on performance. Although, the results suggest that DBMS_LOB.SUBSTR may be a viable alternative when needing to perform SUBSTR on CLOB data types. Overall, foremost to consider performance factors when working with large text data in PL/SQL procedures, and to choose the appropriate data type and method to optimize performance.]]>

item.title: Oracle Ora 00923 From Keyword Missing A Common Database Error
item.description:
ORACLE: ORA-00923: FROM keyword missing - A Common Database Error In this error (ORA-00923: FROM keyword not found where expected), the issue seems to be with the SQL query syntax. The error message indicates that the Oracle SQL parser is expecting a “FROM” keyword but it is not found where it is expected.

Let’s take a closer look at the SQL query in question:

select 
  country_olympic_name, 
  SUM(part_gold) as "Number of Gold Medals"
From
  games.country,
  games.participation
where
  participation.country_isocode = country.country_isocode
group by
  country_olympic_name;

				  The SQL query is attempting to retrieve the number of gold medals won by each country in the "games" table. Although, there is an issue with the syntax.  The error message indicates that the problem is with the "FROM" keyword. Looking at the query, we can see that the "FROM" keyword is missing. Instead, there are two tables, "games.country" and "games.participation", separated by a comma. This is causing confusion for the Oracle SQL parser, which is expecting a "FROM" keyword to indicate where the query is retrieving data from.  To fix this error, we need to add a "FROM" keyword to the SQL query. We can also remove the comma and replace it with a join statement, which will make the query easier to read and know:  
				  

select 
  country_olympic_name, 
  SUM(part_gold) as "Number of Gold Medals"
FROM
  games.country
INNER JOIN
  games.participation
ON
  participation.country_isocode = country.country_isocode
GROUP BY
  country_olympic_name;

In the revised SQL query, we have added a “FROM” keyword and replaced the comma with an inner join statement. We have also added an “ON” keyword to specify the join condition between the two tables. To summarize, the ORA-00923 error occurs when the Oracle SQL parser cannot find a “FROM” keyword where it is expected. To fix this error, we need to ensure that our SQL query contains a “FROM” keyword and that the syntax is correct. In this case, we replaced the comma with a join statement to improve the readability and clarity of the query. item.title: Oracle Oracle 9I Treating Empty Strings As Null
item.description:
ORACLE: Oracle 9i: Treating Empty Strings as NULL Summary:

Oracle 9i treats an empty string as NULL, which goes against the SQL standard that considers them as distinct entities. The reason behind this behavior is that Oracle made this design decision before the SQL standard came around, and changing it could break existing code. Thus, Oracle chose to violate the SQL standard rather than disrupting its users.

Explanation:

Back in the olden days before there was a SQL standard, Oracle made the design decision that empty strings in VARCHAR/VARCHAR2 columns were NULL, and there was only one sense of NULL. By the time the SQL standard came around and agreed that NULL and the empty string were distinct entities, Oracle users had code that assumed that the two were equivalent.

Yes, it is possible to perform a bitwise group function in SQL.

For example, if you have a table with bitwise flags, you can use the BIT_OR function in MySQL to perform a bitwise OR operation on all the values in a group.

Here’s an example query in MySQL:

SELECT user_id, BIT_OR(permissions) as all_perms
FROM permissions
GROUP BY user_id

This will return a result set that shows the user ID and the bitwise OR of all the permissions for that user.

item.title: Oracle Resolving Ora 01008 Error Your Bound Variables
item.description:
ORACLE: Resolving the ORA-01008 Error: Your Bound Variables Summary: The query runs successfully in Oracle SQL developer but throws an error (ORA-01008: not all variables bound) when executed in .NET. The developer has tried various ways of binding the variables, changing the data types, and using literals instead of binding.

Query:

SELECT rf.myrow floworder, rf.stage, rf.prss,
rf.pin instnum, rf.prid, r_history.rt, r_history.wt
FROM
(
    SELECT sub2.myrow, sub2.stage, sub2.prss, sub2.pin, sub2.prid
    FROM (
        SELECT sub.myrow, sub.stage, sub.prss, sub.pin,
            sub.prid, MAX(sub.target_rn) OVER (ORDER BY sub.myrow) target_row
            ,sub.hflag
        FROM (
            WITH floc AS 
            (
                SELECT flow.prss, flow.seq_num
                FROM rpf@mydblink flow
                WHERE flow.parent_p = :lapp
                AND flow.prss IN (
                    SELECT r_priprc.prss
                    FROM r_priprc@mydblink r_priprc
                    WHERE priprc = :lot_priprc
                )
                AND rownum = 1
            )
            SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY pp.seq_num, rpf.seq_num) myrow,
            pp.stage, pp.prss, pp.seq_num AS "PIN", rpf.prid, rpf.rn, rpf.target_rn,
            DECODE(floc.seq_num,NULL,0,1) hflag
            FROM rpf@mydblink rpf, pp@mydblink pp, floc
            WHERE rpf.pin = pp.seq_num
            AND rpf.prss = pp.prss
            AND rpf.parent_p = :lapp
            AND pp.parent_p = :lapp
            AND rpf.prss = floc.prss(+)
            AND rpf.seq_num <= floc.seq_num(+)
            AND rpf.target_prid IS NOT NULL ORDER BY myrow
        )sub --sub
    )sub2 --sub2
)rf, --from rf
(SELECT r.pin, MAX(decode(r.transaction_type,'prod','DFLT',r.transaction_type)) AS RT,
MAX(r.transaction_timestamp) AS WT FROM
( SELECT trn.*,max(trn.transaction_timestamp) over (partition by trn.pin) tmax
    FROM r_trans@mydblink trn
    ) r
WHERE r.tmax = r.transaction_timestamp
AND r.parent_p = :lapp
GROUP BY r.pin)r_history --inner join
WHERE rf.pin=r_history.pin(+)
AND rf.stage != :rplstg
ORDER BY floworder

Problem:

The error “ORA-01008: not all variables bound” occurs when trying to execute the query in .NET, while it runs successfully in Oracle SQL developer. The developer has tried changing the data types, binding variables in different ways, and using literals instead of binding but the problem persists.

item.description:
ORACLE: Setting Variables in SQL Select Statement

Declaring and Setting Variables in a Select Statement in Oracle

In Oracle, the SQL and PL/SQL are two different languages with separate engines. Therefore, it is not possible to declare and set variables in a select statement like in SQL Server.

Although, you can use anonymous PL/SQL blocks to declare variables and then use them in a select statement. Here’s an example:

DECLARE 
  v_date1 DATE := to_date('03-AUG-2010', 'DD-Mon-YYYY');
BEGIN
  SELECT U.VisualID
  FROM Usage U
  WHERE U.UseTime > v_date1;
END;
/

In this example, we first declare a variable called v_date1 and set its value. We then use this variable in the select statement to retrieve the VisualID from the Usage table where the UseTime is greater than v_date1.

item.title: Oracle Short Circuit Evaluation Does It Use It
item.description:
Oracle and Short-Circuit Evaluation: Does it Use It? Does Oracle use short-circuit evaluation?
When writing Oracle queries, it’s important to know how the optimizer evaluates predicates in the WHERE clause. One common question is whether or not Oracle uses short-circuit evaluation, meaning that it stops evaluating predicates once it knows the outcome.

What is short-circuit evaluation?

Short-circuit evaluation is the process by which a program evaluates the parts of a Boolean expression only as far as necessary to determine the final outcome. For example, in the expression x && y, if x is false, there’s no need to evaluate y since the expression will always be false. Similarly, in the expression x || y, if x is true, there’s no need to evaluate y since the expression will always be true. This can be a useful optimization when evaluating complex expressions or when evaluating expensive or time-consuming predicates.

item.title: Oracle Should You Use Char Or Byte For Varchar2n Default

ORACLE: Should You Use CHAR or BYTE for varchar2(n) Default? Learning the Default Mode of varchar2 in Oracle
When you declare a varchar2 type in Oracle but don’t explicitly specify whether to use BYTE or CHAR, the default mode will depend on the NLS_LENGTH_SEMANTICS parameter. By default, this parameter is set to BYTE, which means that if you declare a varchar2(500), Oracle will allocate 500 bytes for that field.

What is the Difference Between BYTE and CHAR in varchar2?

The difference between BYTE and CHAR in varchar2 is in how the length of the field is calculated. When you use BYTE, Oracle allocates the exact number of bytes that you specify, regardless of the character set. This can be problematic if you are using a variable-length character set like AL32UTF8, as some characters may require more than one byte of storage.

What is RowID?

RowID is a physical address that uniquely identifies a row in a database table. It is stored as a 6-byte binary value that describes the file number, block number, and slot number of the row. RowIDs are generated automatically by Oracle and are used internally by the database to locate rows quickly.

item.title: Oracle Troubleshooting No Data Found Error In Pl Sql Blocks
item.description:
ORACLE: Troubleshooting No Data Found Error in PL/SQL Blocks PL/SQL Block Problem: No data found error In this Q&A Session, we will discuss the problem of “No data found” error that occurs in a PL/SQL block when a SELECT statement returns no records. We will also provide a solution to handle this error gracefully.

The Problem

Suppose we have the following PL/SQL block:

SET SERVEROUTPUT ON
DECLARE
    v_student_id NUMBER := &sv_student_id;
    v_section_id NUMBER := 89;
    v_final_grade NUMBER;
    v_letter_grade CHAR(1);
BEGIN
    SELECT final_grade
    INTO v_final_grade
    FROM enrollment
    WHERE student_id = v_student_id
    AND section_id = v_section_id;

    CASE -- outer CASE
        WHEN v_final_grade IS NULL THEN
            DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE ('There is no final grade.');
        ELSE
            CASE -- inner CASE
                WHEN v_final_grade >= 90 THEN v_letter_grade := 'A';
                WHEN v_final_grade >= 80 THEN v_letter_grade := 'B';
                WHEN v_final_grade >= 70 THEN v_letter_grade := 'C';
                WHEN v_final_grade >= 60 THEN v_letter_grade := 'D';
                ELSE v_letter_grade := 'F';
            END CASE;

            -- control resumes here after inner CASE terminates
            DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE ('Letter grade is: '||v_letter_grade);
    END CASE;
    -- control resumes here after outer CASE terminates
END;

The above code takes a student ID as input and retrieves the final grade for that student from the enrollment table. The final grade is used to calculate a letter grade using a CASE statement. If the final grade is NULL, the block outputs a message saying “There is no final grade.”

item.title: Oracle Truncate A Ddl Statement
item.description:
ORACLE: Truncate: A DDL Statement? Why is truncate a DDL statement?
Truncate is a statement used to remove all the data from a table or a set of partitions, which is faster than deleting each record one by one. Although the table structure remains the same, truncate makes some significant changes that can be confusing. But why is truncate considered a Data Definition Language (DDL) statement?

How to use setDate() in PreparedStatement:

Suppose you have a table in your database with a column of type DATE. You want to insert the current date into this column using PreparedStatement. Here’s how you can do that. First, create a java.util.Date object representing the current date and time: Date now = new Date(); Next, create a java.sql.Date object from the java.util.Date object: java.sql.Date sqlDate = new java.sql.Date(now.getTime()); Now, create your SQL statement with a parameter for the date column: String sql = "INSERT INTO my_table(date_column) VALUES(?)"; Then, create a PreparedStatement object: PreparedStatement pstmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql); Lastly, set the date parameter in the PreparedStatement object using the setDate() method: pstmt.setDate(1, sqlDate); Execute the statement and you’re done! pstmt.executeUpdate();

item.title: Oracle11g How To Create Parameterized Views
item.description:
Oracle11g: How to Create Parameterized Views Summary: In Oracle 11g, you can create parameterized views using the SYS_CONTEXT method. This method involves creating a context and a package for setting and retrieving the parameters. The parameters can then be used in the view query via the SYS_CONTEXT function.

Creating the Context and Package: To create the context and package, you can use the following code:

CREATE CONTEXT context_name USING package_name;

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE package_name IS
  PROCEDURE set_param(param1 datatype, param2 datatype);
  -- add more procedures as needed for additional parameters
END;

CREATE OR REPLACE PACKAGE BODY package_name IS
  PROCEDURE set_param(param1 datatype, param2 datatype) IS
  BEGIN
    DBMS_SESSION.SET_CONTEXT('context_name', 'param1', param1);
    DBMS_SESSION.SET_CONTEXT('context_name', 'param2', param2);
  END;
  -- add more procedures as needed for additional parameters
END;

Replace context_name and package_name with your desired names. Replace datatype with the appropriate data type for each parameter. Add more procedures as needed for additional parameters.

Yes, the closest equivalent datatype in Oracle is System Change Number (SCN).

What is RowVersion datatype in SQL Server and how does it work?

RowVersion is a data type in SQL Server that automatically generates unique binary numbers within a database. It is used as a mechanism for version-stamping table rows. The storage size of RowVersion is 8 bytes. Each database has a counter that is incremented for each insert or update operation that is performed on a table that contains a RowVersion column within the database.

item.title: Oracles Guide To Ddl Transaction Rollback
item.description:
Oracle’s Guide to DDL and Transaction Rollback Is DDL transactional in Oracle?
DDL (Data Definition Language) statements in Oracle, such as Create or Alter, are not transactional. According to Oracle’s official documentation, the database implicitly commits the current transaction before and after every DDL statement. Essentially, DDL statements act as separate transactions to any data modifications that the statement may make. While other transactions may make modifications involving the object being modified in a DDL statement, all these operations will still run in the transaction that includes the DDL statement. If the DDL statement fails or is cancelled, all operations within the transaction including the DDL statement will be rolled back.

How is the query timeout implemented?

The query timeout is implemented in the JDBC driver itself on the client-side. When a statement is executed with a timeout, a statement timeout thread is created. This thread is created only once, no matter how many statements or connections are used. The thread lasts the lifetime of the VM.

SELECT

  u.surname AS user_surname,
  p.name AS parent_name,
  p.surname AS parent_surname
FROM user u
JOIN parent p ON u.parent = p.id

item.title: Querying Sql For Latest Record Date Per User A Guide
item.description:
Querying SQL for Latest Record Date per User: A Guide In this post, we will discuss how to query SQL for the latest record date for each user. This is a common requirement in SQL queries where we need to identify the latest record for each category or group.

Let’s consider a sample table that contains entries of when users logged in with some additional values.

username, date, value
-++ | id | username |        date         | +-+-++ ```  
### Example 1: Using Row Number Window Functions
  ``` SELECT x.username, x.date FROM (     SELECT          username, date,         ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY username ORDER BY date DESC) AS _rn     FROM login_table  ) x WHERE x._rn = 1 ```  Output:  ``` ++ | username |        date         | ++ | alice    | 2021-01-14 09:00:00 | | jane     | 2021-01-13 08:10:10 | | john     | 2021-01-15 10:20:10 | ++ ```  
### Example 2: Using Inner Join
  ``` SELECT t.username, t.date FROM login_table t INNER JOIN (     SELECT username, MAX(date) AS MaxDate     FROM login_table     GROUP BY username ) tm ON t.username = tm.username AND t.date = tm.MaxDate ```  Output:  ``` ++ | username |        date         | ++ | jane     | 2021-01-13 08:10:10 | | john     | 2021-01-15 10:20:10 | | alice    | 2021-01-14 09:00:00 | ++ ```  
### Example 3: Using Left Outer Join
  ``` SELECT a.username, a.date FROM login_table a LEFT OUTER JOIN login_table b ON a.username = b.username  AND a.date < b.date WHERE b.username IS NULL ORDER BY a.date DESC; ```  Output:  ``` ++ | username |        date         | ++ | jane     | 2021-01-13 08:10:10 | | john     | 2021-01-15 10:20:10 | | alice    | 2021-01-14 09:00:00 | ++ ```  
## Recap:
  Querying SQL for the latest date for each group or category is a common requirement. In this post, we discussed different approaches to achieve the same solution using window functions, inner join, and left outer join.   Window functions provide an efficient and useful way to solve this problem. Although, the use of inner join and left outer join is also helpful, considering the syntax and meaning of the query.  Selecting the most viable query depends on your preferences, database engine, and whether or not duplicates exist.]]>

item.title: Randomize Your Data With Sqlites Order By Rand
item.description:
SQLite - ORDER BY RAND() Solution:

Using RANDOM() with SQLite 3
In MySQL, the RAND() function can be used to generate random results from a query. Is there an alternative in SQLite 3?

SQLite 3 provides a similar function called random() :

SELECT foo FROM bar
  WHERE id >= (abs(random()) % (SELECT max(id) FROM bar))
  LIMIT 1;

EDIT (by QOP): Since the documentation on SQLite Autoincrement ed columns states that:

The normal ROWID selection algorithm described above will generate monotonically increasing unique ROWIDs as long as you never use the maximum ROWID value and you never delete the entry in the table with the largest ROWID.   • RENAME TO or Rename TO: This tells Oracle to rename the table or view.
  • [new_table_name]: This is the new name that you want to give to the table or view.

item.title: Resetting A Sequence In Oracle A Quick Guide
item.description:
Resetting a Sequence in Oracle: A Quick Guide How to reset a sequence in Oracle?

To reset a sequence to 0 in Oracle, you can use the following procedure created by Oracle expert Tom Kyte:

create or replace procedure reset_seq( p_seq_name in varchar2 )
is
    l_val number;
begin
    execute immediate
    'select ' || p_seq_name || '.nextval from dual' INTO l_val;

    execute immediate
    'alter sequence ' || p_seq_name || ' increment by -' || l_val || 
                                                          ' minvalue 0';

    execute immediate
    'select ' || p_seq_name || '.nextval from dual' INTO l_val;

    execute immediate
    'alter sequence ' || p_seq_name || ' increment by 1 minvalue 0';
end;
/

This procedure increments the sequence by its current value, sets it to 0, and then increments it once more to set the sequence back to 1.

item.title: Role Of Order By 1 In Sql Select Query
item.description:
The Role of Order By 1 in SQL SELECT Query The purpose of “Order By 1” in SQL Select statement is to sort the results based on the first column returned by the query. In other words, it orders the view or table by the first column of the result set.

For example, in the following code snippet:

SELECT A.PAYMENT_DATE,
   (SELECT SUM(paymentamount)
      FROM payment B
     WHERE PAYMENT_DATE = B.PAYMENT_DATE
       and SOME CONDITION) AS SUM_X,
   (SELECT SUM(paymentamount)
      FROM payment B
     WHERE PAYMENT_DATE = B.PAYMENT_DATE
       and SOME OTHER CONDITION) AS SUM_Y    
FROM payment A    
ORDER BY 1;

“Order By 1” means that the results will be sorted by the first column, which is the payment_date column.

What is an ObjectId?

An ObjectId is a unique identifier for documents stored in MongoDB. It is a 12-byte BSON type that is composed of a 4-byte timestamp, a 3-byte machine identifier, a 2-byte process ID, and a 3-byte counter. ObjectIds are typically used in conjunction with the MongoDB _id field and can be used to uniquely identify documents.

item.title: Selecting Data From Google Bigquery Timestamp Column Within N Days
item.description:
Filtering Records in Google BigQuery Based on Timestamp Columns

Summary

To filter records in Google BigQuery based on a timestamp column between a certain number of days or weeks ago and today, you can use the BETWEEN operator along with the TIMESTAMP_ADD and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP functions to specify the time range.

Code Explanation

To select all records in a BigQuery table sample_table that are 2 weeks old:

SELECT t.*
FROM `my-pj.my_dataset.sample_table` t
WHERE register_date BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_ADD(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL -14 DAY) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
LIMIT 10;
  • The SELECT statement retrieves all columns from sample_table using the alias t. - The WHERE clause filters records based on the register_date column, which is compared to a time range using the BETWEEN operator. - The TIMESTAMP_ADD function calculates a new timestamp by subtracting 14 days from the current timestamp obtained using CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. - The CURRENT_TIMESTAMP function retrieves the current timestamp. - The LIMIT clause limits the number of records returned to 10.

Alternative Ways

item.title: Selecting First Day Of Month In Sql
item.description:
Selecting First Day of Month in SQL In SQL, you can select the first day of a month using various methods. One way is to use the DATEADD and DATEDIFF functions to add or subtract the number of months and days from a given date. Here’s an example:

SELECT DATEADD(month, DATEDIFF(month, 0, GETDATE()), 0) AS StartOfMonth;

				  This query retrieves the current date and time using the GETDATE function and then calculates the number of months between the start of the year (represented by 0) and the current date using the DATEDIFF function. The DATEADD function then adds this number of months to the start of the year and returns the resulting date, which represents the first day of the current month.  Another way to select the first day of a month is to use the DATEFROMPARTS function, which was introduced in SQL Server 2012. This function takes the year, month, and day values as arguments and returns a datetime value. Here's an example:  
				  

SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(GETDATE()), MONTH(GETDATE()), 1) AS StartOfMonth;

This query retrieves the current date and time using the GETDATE function and then uses the YEAR and MONTH functions to extract the year and month values. The function then returns a datetime value that represents the first day of the current month by passing these values to the DATEFROMPARTS function and using 1 as the day argument. You can also use the EOMONTH function, which returns the last day of a month, and then add one day to it to get the first day of the next month. Here’s an example:

Show Running Processes in Oracle DB

To show running processes on an Oracle database, you can use the V$SESSION view to retrieve information about current user sessions running on the database. The following SQL query retrieves the process, status, username, schemaname, and SQL statement for all user sessions:

SELECT sess.process, sess.status, sess.username, sess.schemaname, sql.sql_text
  FROM v$session sess,
       v$sql     sql
 WHERE sql.sql_id(+) = sess.sql_id
   AND sess.type="USER"

The outer join is used to handle inactive sessions that may not have an associated SQL statement. You can also use the V$SQL view to retrieve the full SQL statement for each session by replacing sql.sql_text with sql.sql_fulltext.

item.title: Sql Choosing Multiple Rows Of Consistent Data A Guide
item.description:
SQL: Choosing Multiple Rows of Consistent Data: A Guide In SQL, selecting constants without referencing a table is legal. It means you can use constant values to create a result set without using a table. For instance, you can use the following SQL statement to select constant values:

SELECT 1, 2, 3;

				  The above statement will return a single row containing the constant values 1, 2, and 3. But what if you wanted to select multiple rows at once using a constant expression? This is where the `UNION ALL` clause comes in handy.  The `UNION ALL` clause allows you to combine the results of two or more SELECT statements into a single result set. You can use the `UNION ALL` operator to combine multiple SELECT statements that use constant expressions to produce a result set with multiple rows and columns.   For example, the following SQL statement uses the `UNION ALL` operator to combine three SELECT statements that use constant expressions:  
				  

SELECT 1, 2, 3
UNION ALL SELECT 4, 5, 6
UNION ALL SELECT 7, 8, 9;

The above SQL statement produces a result set with three rows and three columns, containing the values (1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6), and (7, 8, 9). There are other ways to select multiple rows using constant expressions in different SQL database management systems. For instance, in Oracle, you can use the CONNECT BY clause to generate a recordset of arbitrary number of rows. item.title: Sql Precision Scale For Storing Money In Decimal Columns
item.description: SQL: Precision and Scale for Storing Money in Decimal Columns Summary: When storing money values in a database using a decimal column, foremost to consider the precision and scale. A popular choice for the precision and scale is DECIMAL(19, 4), which originates from the old VBA/Access/Jet Currency data type. This allows for enough decimal places to account for rounding and custom algorithms. Although, if more precision is required, a higher scale can be used. Q: Why use a decimal column to store money values in a database? A: A decimal column allows for more precise calculations and avoids the limitations of floating-point arithmetic. Q: What precision and scale should be used for a decimal column storing money values? A: A popular choice is DECIMAL(19, 4), which allows for enough decimal places to account for rounding and custom algorithms. Although, if more precision is required, a higher scale can be used. Q: Why is an extra decimal place in storage recommended for a decimal column? A: An extra decimal place allows for a custom rounding algorithm to be implemented, rather than relying on the vendor’s default behavior. It also ensures that rounding errors are minimized. Q: Why is DECIMAL(24, 8) not recommended for storing money values? A: It is likely overkill for most currencies, which are quoted to four or five decimal places. It may also result in unnecessary storage space and potential rounding errors. Practical Example: Suppose a transaction table in a database needs to store money values in multiple currencies. One option is to store the conversion rates (when applicable) in the transaction table itself, as a float, and store the currency in the account table. The transaction amount can then be stored as a DECIMAL(19, 4), which allows for enough precision to handle rounding and custom algorithms. Alternative Way: If more precision is required, a higher scale can be used. For example, DECIMAL(24, 8) may be appropriate in some cases. Although, foremost to consider the specific requirements and limitations of the application before choosing a precision and scale.]]>

item.title: Sql Servers Countif Aggregate Function You Need
item.description:
SQL Server’s COUNTIF: The Aggregate Function You Need A common requirement in SQL queries is to count records based on certain conditions. In Microsoft SQL Server, the equivalent of the COUNTIF function from Excel is not directly available. Although, there are several ways to achieve this functionality.

Let’s consider the following example query:

SELECT UID, 
  COUNT(UID) AS TotalRecords, 
  SUM(ContractDollars) AS ContractDollars,
  (COUNTIF(MyColumn, 1) / COUNT(UID) * 100) 
FROM dbo.AD_CurrentView
GROUP BY UID
HAVING SUM(ContractDollars) >= 500000

				  In this query, we have a GROUP BY clause that needs to count records based only on a certain condition, such as counting records where a certain column value is equal to 1. The above query is trying to determine the percentage of all rows that have the value 1 in the MyColumn column.  Let's explore some ways to achieve this functionality:  Using SUM and CASE  One way to count records based on a condition is by using the SUM function with a CASE statement. We can write the following query:  
				  

SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN MyColumn = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) 
FROM dbo.AD_CurrentView

In this query, we are using the CASE statement to check if the value in the MyColumn column is equal to 1. If it is, we add 1 to the sum. Otherwise, we add 0 to the sum. This way, we are effectively counting the number of records that satisfy a condition. item.title: Sql Updating Multiple Columns Made Simple
item.description:
SQL: Updating Multiple Columns Made Simple How to Update Multiple Columns in SQL Server?

Updating multiple columns in SQL Server is possible using the UPDATE statement. It allows you to set multiple columns to new values based on some condition. Here’s an example of how to update multiple columns using the same syntax as the insert statement.

Syntax:

UPDATE table_name
SET column_name1 = new_value1, column_name2 = new_value2, ..., column_nameN = new_valueN
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;

				  Let's assume that we have two tables - Table1 and Table2 - which have some columns that contain the same data. We would like to update Table1 columns with Table2 values, based on a common ID column. Here is how you can do that:  
				  

UPDATE Table1
SET Table1.a = Table2.a,
    Table1.b = Table2.b,
    Table1.c = Table2.c,
    Table1.d = Table2.d,
    Table1.e = Table2.e,
    Table1.f = Table2.f,
    Table1.g = Table2.g,
    Table1.h = Table2.h,
    Table1.i = Table2.i,
    Table1.j = Table2.j,
    Table1.k = Table2.k
FROM Table1
INNER JOIN Table2 ON Table1.ID = Table2.ID;

Explanation: - The UPDATE statement begins by specifying the target table (Table1). - The SET clause assigns new values to the columns we want to update, using the values from Table2. - The FROM clause specifies the second table (Table2) from which we’ll get the new values. - The INNER JOIN clause joins the two tables based on the common ID column. - The WHERE clause defines the condition under which the update will take place. The above code can be challenging to write and maintain, especially when dealing with many columns. In such cases, visual tools like SQL Server Management Studio can generate update statements automatically. item.title: Sql Using Case Statement In A Join Condition
item.description:
SQL: Using CASE Statement in a JOIN Condition? Can I use CASE statement in a JOIN condition?

Yes, but the syntax should be different. A CASE expression returns a value from the THEN portion of the clause, so you need to do something with the returned value, e.g. compare it to 1. Here is an example:

SELECT  * 
FROM    sys.indexes i 
JOIN    sys.partitions p ON i.index_id = p.index_id  
JOIN    sys.allocation_units a 
ON      (CASE WHEN a.type IN (1, 3) AND a.container_id = p.hobt_id THEN 1
              WHEN a.type IN (2) AND a.container_id = p.partition_id THEN 1
              ELSE 0
         END) = 1

Note that you need to wrap the CASE expression in parentheses and add an alias to the JOIN condition that compares it to 1. Also, the returned value should be a numeric value, not an assignment or test for equality.

Any operation involving NULL evaluates to NULL, including arithmetic, comparison, and concatenation operations.

What is the difference between != and <> in SQL?

The != and <> operators are equivalent in SQL and are used to compare two values to see if they are not equal. Although, they cannot be used to compare with NULL since NULL is not a value, but rather a placeholder to indicate the absence of a value. Therefore, when you use != or <> to compare a value with NULL, the result is always NULL, and you get no rows as a result.

item.title: Subquery Check In Oracle Streamlining Data Validation
item.description:

When working with Oracle, it can be quite frustrating to learn that the CHECK constraint does not allow subqueries. Fortunately, there are several ways to work around this limitation.

The Problem

Let’s look at the example code:

CREATE TABLE Tank (
    n_id            int,
    day             date,
    level           int,
    CONSTRAINT pk_w_td PRIMARY KEY (n_id,day),
    CONSTRAINT fk_w_td_tan FOREIGN KEY (n_id) REFERENCES Tanks ON DELETE CASCADE,
    CHECK (level > 0 AND level <= (SELECT capacity FROM Tanks WHERE Tanks.n_id = TanksDay.n_id))
);

In this example, we have a table called “Tank” with three columns: n_id, day, and level. We have a primary key constraint on n_id and day and a foreign key constraint on n_id. Lastly, we have a CHECK constraint that prevents the level from exceeding the capacity of the tank referenced by n_id.

item.title: Subtracting 1 Day From A Timestamp Date In Sql
item.description:
Subtracting 1 Day from a Timestamp Date in SQL In this SQL query, we are working with PostgreSQL and trying to subtract 1 day from a timestamp date, filter it based on a time window of today-130 days, and display it without the hh/mm/ss part of the stamp (2016-10-31). Let’s break down the query:

select org_id, count(accounts) as count, ((date_at) - 1) as dateat 
from sourcetable 
where  date_at <= now() - 130
group by org_id, dateat

				  - Line 1: We are selecting `org_id`, counting `accounts` and subtracting 1 day from `date_at`. Although, PostgreSQL doesn't allow subtracting an integer from a timestamp without a type cast. - Line 2: We are filtering the table by `date_at` less than or equal to 130 days ago from the current date and time (now). - Line 3: We are grouping the results by `org_id` and `date_at` minus 1 day and aliasing the result as `dateat`.  To solve the error of subtracting an integer from a timestamp without a type cast, we can use the `INTERVAL` type to subtract 1 day. Here's the updated query:  
				  

SELECT org_id, COUNT(accounts) AS count, (date_at - INTERVAL '1 DAY') AS dateat 
FROM sourcetable 
WHERE date_at <= NOW() - INTERVAL '130 DAYS'
GROUP BY org_id, dateat::date
  • Line 1: We are selecting org_id, counting accounts and subtracting 1 day from date_at using the INTERVAL type. - Line 2: We are filtering the table by date_at less than or equal to 130 days ago from the current date and time (now) using the INTERVAL type. - Line 3: We are grouping the results by org_id and dateat cast as a date using the ::date syntax to display it without the hh/mm/ss part of the stamp.

Tips:

  • Tip 1: You can append multiple operands to an interval. For example, to get the last day of the current month use date_trunc('MONTH', CURRENT_DATE) + INTERVAL '1 MONTH - 1 DAY'. - Tip 2: You can create an interval using the make_interval function. References: - PostgreSQL Date/Time Functions: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/functions-datetime.html]]>

Sorry, as an AI language model, I don’t have the ability to provide you with an exact answer to this question. Although, I can provide you with a general idea of SQL anti-patterns.

SQL anti-patterns are practices that do more harm than good in SQL programming. Some of the most common SQL anti-patterns include:

  1. Using SELECT * instead of specifying required columns in the query
  2. Using nested queries or subqueries without proper indexing
  3. Using correlated subqueries or cursors instead of set-based logic
  4. Using scalar or aggregate functions unnecessarily in SELECT or WHERE clauses
  5. Using string concatenation instead of parameterized queries for dynamic SQL
  6. Using inconsistent data types for columns or parameters
  7. Using hard-coded values instead of using variables or parameters
  8. Not using primary keys, foreign keys, or unique constraints in tables
  9. Not normalizing tables or using denormalized data
  10. Using triggers or stored procedures when not necessary or misusing them

To avoid SQL anti-patterns, it is recommended to follow best practices and guidelines for SQL programming, use standard SQL syntax, normalize tables properly, and optimize queries for performance. ]]>
